## Assessment

This refreshed reconciliation includes the approved changes. The [upstream history since the previous review](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/compare/5863806dd4e15c63174bee4e7515a4256792ecfa...6f7f7831a625f040a8e06a0e7954826b87ce775a) contains no skill removals and no changes under upstream `docs/`.

### Adopted

- `software-factory` now quotes its description; the fork diff shows only user-only invocation metadata. Also quoted the same invalid YAML form in the local `clean-copy` draft. The installer-compatible checker uses pinned `yaml`, rejects malformed frontmatter, duplicate keys, and missing or blank names and descriptions, and runs in CI for both the promoted and draft roots. Existing plugin validators remain independent.
- `domain-modeling` now bolds exact canonical terms inside definitions to express relationships. The examples match upstream; the remaining skill delta is equivalent rule wording. The published guide teaches the same convention.
- `chief-of-staff` now delegates to fresh workers while keeping the user conversation in the main session. It keeps a dated, source-cited wiki and proposes environment changes only after observed friction. Its draft index, Codex picker text, and router entry reflect the new workflow. Unlike upstream, the fork asks the user to invoke auxiliary user-only procedures and requires approval for environment changes and schedules.
- The approved documentation improvements now illustrate Standards versus Spec in `code-review`, portability versus compaction in `handoff`, fact-finding versus decisions in `grilling`, and the survey-to-build boundary in `improve-codebase-architecture`. Each reflects the local skill rather than replacing it with upstream prose.

----
-name: clean-copy
-description: "Cut interface copy that shouldn't exist: captions that restate a label, hints that pre-empt a worry the user never had, warnings that are scar tissue from a fixed bug. Use when writing or reviewing any user-facing string (labels, hints, empty states, toasts, confirmations, button text), or when asked to clean up / tighten copy."
----
-
-# Cleaning copy
-
-Most bad copy isn't badly written. It's copy that shouldn't be on the screen. Editing it for
-tone just makes the wrong thing read better. So the first question is never "how should this
-be phrased". It's **should this exist**.
-
-## The ladder
-
-Walk a string down these in order. Stop at the first one that fires and delete.
-
-**1. Does this need to surface at all?**
-Is the thing being described something the user would ever have wondered about, unprompted? If
-they'd never have thought to ask, you're not answering a question. You're planting one. Nobody
-opens an avatar cropper wondering whether the circle is a true circle. A caption reading "the
-preview is rendered at the exact size used on your profile" makes them wonder whether it might
-not be.
-
-**2. Does the label need to exist?**
-A caption earns its place only when the value is meaningless without it. If the label, the
-field, or the value beside it already says the thing, the caption is noise. A field labelled
-"Retry limit" does not need "how many times we retry" beneath it. A bare "30" does need
-"seconds" beside it; that one stays.
-
-**3. Is it pre-empting something the user would never have had to consider?**
-The tell: copy that rules out a failure rather than describing a behaviour.
-
-> Cancel upload
-> *Always keeps the files already transferred; never wipes the folder like the old cancel did.*
-
-That second clause exists because of a bug. The user doesn't know about the bug, doesn't share
-your memory of fixing it, and now has a worry they arrived without. **The fix for a fixed bug
-is the fix. Not a caption about the fix.** Same for copy defending a design decision, or
-hedging about something that simply works: "this may look slow but it is not", "don't worry if
-the count seems off for a moment".
-
-**4. Rewrite to remove the offending part. If nothing is left, delete the element.**
-Don't preserve a hint just because there was a hint there. An empty `hint` prop comes off the
-component; an explanatory `<p>` gets deleted, not shortened to a stub.
-
-## What survives
-
-Copy stays when the user genuinely cannot act without it:
-
-- A real consequence at the moment of choosing. Under a destructive button: *"Anything not yet
-  synced is lost."* They need it before they click, and they can't infer it.
-- A compatibility or scope fact they can't see. *"Works with keys issued after March; older
-  keys need rotating first."* The checkbox alone doesn't tell them whether it applies to them.
-- What a blank state means and what to do next. *"No projects yet. Create one and it will
-  appear here."*
-- Units, scale, or format on a bare value.
-
-Note the first example is one sentence. Had it continued *"; only use this when a sync is
-stuck"*, that half would go: it instructs the user on when they're allowed to press a button
-they can already see. Keep the consequence, cut the permission slip.
-
-## Working style
-
-- Read the string next to what's actually on screen around it: the label, the value, the
-  button. Redundancy is invisible when you read the string alone.
-- Cut whole clauses, not words. Tightening "Leave this blank to use the default setting for
-  your account" into "Leave blank for the default" is a smaller win than noticing which half of
-  a two-sentence hint is doing no work.
-- When reviewing a batch, report as `file:line` with the current string and either the rewrite
-  or `cut`, and say in a few words which rung it failed. Don't rewrite copy that passes.
-- If a string is load-bearing but only in a rare state, consider whether it belongs in that
-  state rather than permanently on the page.
-
~~~~

-# Pruning campaign
-
-Use for a whole subsystem or repository. Apply the [value bar](SKILL.md#value-bar) and [audit guide](references/audit.md); this sequence replaces the local audit sequence.
-
-## 1. Baseline and lanes
-
-Record the source revision and known test results. Run uncovered in-scope suites to establish their baseline; preserve user-reported failures as evidence rather than rerunning to confirm them. Separate product failures from pruning work.
-
-Inventory all owned test files, parameter tables, shared-boundary coverage, and live or QA scenarios. Assign each to one **lane** by production owner, not filename prefix. Shared harnesses have one integration owner.
-
-Done when every test surface belongs to one lane and has a recorded baseline result or explicit execution limitation.
-
-## 2. Read-only ledger
-
-Read each lane's tests and production paths using the audit guide. Record a classification and evidence for every declaration, splitting parameter rows when necessary. Keep discovery read-only until all lanes are accounted for. Independent lanes may be investigated in parallel.
-
-Done when every declaration and QA scenario has a ledger entry, including unresolved evidence.
-
-## 3. Layer plan
-
-Review the ledger by contract rather than treating it as a deletion list. Identify redundant layers and name each keeper, the assertions it must absorb, retired files, distinct boundary risks that remain, and obsolete support or production seams.
-
-Done when each lane has an evidence-backed cutover plan and every retained contract has a keeper. Exclude unresolved candidates from deletion.
-
-## 4. Cutover
-
-Apply the plan lane by lane, transferring unique assertions before removals. Serialize shared-harness changes through the integration owner. Update affected CI routing and test inventories. Check remaining callers before removing obsolete support and production seams.
-
-Run the affected keepers after each lane's cutover; batch edits before each check rather than checking every individual edit.
-
-Done when every lane plan is applied and its keepers pass or recorded baseline failures remain accounted for.
-
-## 5. Preservation review
-
-Have an independent reviewer compare deleted coverage against keepers, using the ledger and actual assertions. Review by boundary group; look for lost contracts, unreachable negative cases, and fixture-supplied outcomes. If independent review is unavailable, report that limit and perform a separate preservation pass.
-
-Resolve each finding with restored proof or source-backed rejection. Apply the local workflow's [verification requirements](SKILL.md#4-verify-and-report) to repaired assertions, transferred coverage, and any contracts restored during review.
-
-Done when every finding has a disposition and every repaired or transferred contract has a failing control and passing keeper. Report unavailable proof as an incomplete verification item.
-
-## 6. Reconcile and hand off
-
-If the source revision changed during the campaign, inspect intervening changes in affected owners and tests. Port newly added unique contracts into keepers before retiring their old homes, then rerun only affected proof and required repository checks.
-
-Report lanes, retired layers, keepers, preservation findings, removed seams, unresolved candidates, and validation evidence. Count production, test, and support changes separately if reporting size; deletion totals are outcomes, not targets.
-
-Done when every planned lane and intervening contract is accounted for, with execution and review limitations stated explicitly.
~~~~

</details>

----
-name: prune-tests
-description: Remove redundant or behavior-free tests while preserving independent contracts.

----
-
-# Prune Tests
-
-Prune proof that earns no protection. Optimize for contracts preserved with less coupling, not deletion counts.
-
-## Value bar
-
-Each retained test names a **contract** (observable behavior or invariant) and a credible **regression** it detects. A **keeper** is the primary test that proves a contract at its owning production boundary. Another layer earns proof for a distinct boundary risk, such as serialization, persistence, or lifecycle.
-
-Preserve independent API, protocol, storage, migration, security, packaging, and observable-ordering contracts. Static checks, negative assertions, and slow tests can protect real behavior. A baseline failure may be a product defect; preserve its evidence.
-
-Missing evidence means preserve the candidate. Transfer unique coverage to a keeper before deleting its old home.
-
-Before classifying candidates, read [the audit guide](references/audit.md) for evidence requirements, junk patterns, and retention exceptions.
-
-For whole-subsystem or repository-wide pruning, follow [campaign mode](CAMPAIGN.md) instead of the local sequence below. The value bar and audit guide apply in both modes.
-
-## 1. Inventory
-
-Use the requested scope, or the current change when no path is given. If neither identifies tests, ask for a scope. Read every in-scope test, including parameter rows, and the production paths its assertions exercise. Group tests by their production owner.
-
-Classify each declaration using the audit guide. Split parameter rows when their classifications differ.
-
-Done when every in-scope test has a classification and evidence, including explicit unresolved candidates.
-
-## 2. Choose keepers
-
-Map each contract to its keeper. For every proposed removal, name the proof that remains or establish that no intended contract exists. Identify assertions that must move, support code that becomes unused, and distinct risks that justify multiple layers.
-
-Done when every removal has an evidence-backed disposition and every unique contract has a keeper. Preserve unresolved candidates.
-
-## 3. Prune
-
-Repair or transfer unique assertions first, using independent expectations and the real production owner. Then delete redundant or behavior-free tests.
-
-Remove support code and production seams made obsolete by the pruning after checking their remaining callers. Update affected test discovery and CI routing using existing repository conventions.
-
-Done when every planned change is applied and retained proof remains runnable.
-
-## 4. Verify and report
-
-Run affected keeper and sibling suites using the repository's existing commands. Exercise the owning executable when removing static checks that previously supplied its only proof.
-
-For repaired assertions or transferred unique coverage, demonstrate sensitivity to the named regression using a pre-fix baseline or a temporary production mutation. Confirm failure comes from the intended assertion. Restore only your mutation, preserving unrelated edits, and run the keeper on restored production code. Report unavailable baseline proof rather than claiming it.
-
-Report removals and repairs, keeper locations, removed test-only seams, validation results, and unresolved candidates. Separate pre-existing failures from changes caused by pruning; unresolved proof is a completion limit.
-
-Done when affected proof passes, or pre-existing failures are accounted for, and each repaired or transferred contract has a demonstrated failing control and passing keeper.
~~~~

-# Audit guide
-
-## Candidate evidence
-
-Before proposing a repair, consolidation, or deletion, read the full test, production owner, entry points, relevant callers and callees, overlapping tests, and CI routing. Inspect relevant history to establish why the test exists. Check dependency source or types when the judgment depends on dependency behavior.
-
-Record each candidate's:
-
-- Exact name and location, asserted contract, and detectable regression.
-- Non-test callers of any production seam the removal could retire.
-- Keeper location and distinct risks, or evidence that no intended contract exists.
-- Assertions to transfer before removal, including exceptional parameter rows.
-- Relevant history, uncertainty, and focused validation command.
-
-When evidence is unavailable, record the gap and preserve the candidate.
-
-## Classification
-
-- **Keep:** name the contract and credible regression it detects.
-- **Repair:** retain the contract; identify ineffective or misleading proof and its replacement.
-- **Consolidate:** name the keeper and assertions it must absorb before removal.
-- **Delete:** name the remaining proof or establish that no intended contract exists.
-- **Unresolved:** name missing evidence and preserve the test.
-
-Judge assertions rather than names. A test named for persistence may inspect a mock store that production never writes.
-
-## Junk patterns
-
-Treat these as candidates, not automatic deletion rules:
-
-- Self-comparisons, assertion-free probes, and expectations generated by the subject under test.
-- Mocks or fixtures that implement the outcome production is supposed to produce.
-- Private-state, helper-call, internal-order, and source-shape assertions that fail under behavior-preserving refactors.
-- Repeated cases or layers with no distinct failure mode.
-- Copied manifests, export inventories, or constants with no independent contract.
-- Tests asserting removed code stays absent solely because it was removed.
-- Tests repeating guarantees supplied entirely by a dependency or type checker.
-- Negative cases that fail at an unrelated guard or never reach the intended rejection.
-- Fixtures that fabricate receipts, callback order, or persistence effects the owner should produce.
-
-## Retention exceptions
-
-A suspicious form can still protect an independent contract:
-
-- **Absence:** an unsafe API remaining unavailable can be a security requirement. A module remaining absent from its old path is usually migration history, unless that path itself carries a compatibility requirement.
-- **Source or byte checks:** exact protocol bytes, published package contents, architectural boundaries, and generated cross-language interfaces can require static proof. Prefer checks that survive identifier-only refactors unless the identifier is itself public.
-- **Multiple layers:** a domain test and an HTTP test can share a business outcome while catching different defects. Name the transport or lifecycle risk before consolidating them.
-- **Observable calls and order:** charging a payment provider once or acknowledging only after durable storage can be public contracts. Internal helper selection is not the same thing.
-- **Dependencies and types:** verifying a library repeats its own guarantee adds little; verifying our configuration or integration honors that guarantee can earn a keeper. Compile-time tests can protect a published type API.
-- **Test support:** fixtures and teardown can provide necessary isolation. Remove helpers and production seams only when their remaining consumers and contracts are accounted for.
-
-## Examples
-
-**Duplicate or distinct?** Two tests compute the same cart total through the same domain API with equivalent inputs: consolidate. An HTTP test also proves decimal serialization: retain that distinct contract.
-
-**Fabricated or independent?** Mocking `checkout` to return `confirmed` and asserting that result proves the mock. Supplying a payment-provider response and asserting that real checkout produces a retrievable order exercises production behavior.
-
-**Historical or required absence?** A check that `legacy.ts` is gone records a past edit. A package-contents check that excludes private credentials protects an ongoing release contract.
-
~~~~

</details>

----
-name: blast-radius
-description: "Check what a risky change could break beyond the diff and test the safety assumption on real code. Use when asked for the blast radius or when a change can affect downstream consumers, shared state, or durable data."
----
-
-# Blast radius
-
-Test the one fact a material change relies on to be safe. This is a focused risk check, not a Spec or Standards pass or an application-wide verification run.
-
-## 1. Fix the scope
-
-- **Called from review:** Accept the caller's pinned base, reviewed revision, and exact diff scope. Use those inputs as supplied, with no floating-ref substitution or expansion to the working tree.
-- **Standalone:** Identify the requested change and base or before-state, then pin the comparison and state it. Resolve named revisions to commit IDs. If the user specifies staged or working-tree changes, include those exact layers and applicable new files; record that source state before checking. If materially different comparisons are plausible and the request does not distinguish them, ask which change to assess.
-
-Read source from the scoped revision or snapshot, not whichever files happen to be checked out. Keep the user's checkout, refs, index, and product code untouched. If the active workspace does not exactly match the scoped source, use an isolated source snapshot and verify that the source and dependencies used by the check are the scoped ones, including relevant versions or patches. If you cannot inspect or run the right source, report that limit rather than substituting a different revision.
-
-## 2. Trace the failure and state the assumption
-
-Read the diff and follow the changed behavior through the actual boundary. Trace indirect consumers: readers of the same format or durable data, users of shared state or resources, and dependencies on ordering or timing. Follow pinned dependency code or local patches when they decide what happens at the boundary. Direct callers alone are not the boundary when the effect propagates through data, state, or time.
-
-Describe where the break would surface, under what conditions, and what it would cost. Turn the material path into one falsifiable safety assumption: a fact that, if false, would make the identified failure possible. Name the observable result that would distinguish support from contradiction before choosing a check.
-
-## 3. Run the smallest safe check
-
-Use the smallest focused test, command, or throwaway harness that drives the real caller or boundary on the scoped source and would fail if the assumption were false. Reuse existing evidence only if it exercises that same behavior on that exact revision or snapshot. A mocked boundary, a nearby passing test, or a run on different source cannot establish the assumption.
-
-Keep any scratch harness and side effects isolated and temporary; leave no permanent product writes and do not run against live or shared data. If a safe check is unavailable, the right source cannot be isolated, or the run is inconclusive, mark the assumption **Unproven** and state what evidence is missing. End the check once you have a discriminating observation or can name the blocker. Do not add a review pass.
-
-## 4. Report
-
-- **Scope and effect:** Exact comparison, what changed, and which indirect boundary matters. Cite paths and lines or symbols.
-- **Safety assumption:** The fact under test, the exact command (or reference to qualifying existing evidence), the observed result, and the verdict: **Supports**, **Contradicts**, or **Unproven**. For **Unproven**, give the missing evidence and, if known, the smallest next check.
-- **Confirmed:** Failure paths established by evidence, with the boundary, triggering conditions, and impact.
-- **Cleared:** Specific failure paths ruled out by evidence, with the conditions under which they were cleared.
-- **Unchecked:** Plausible paths not resolved by this check and what would resolve them. A gap is not a confirmed risk or a clearance.
-
-When called from review, return this evidence separately from Spec and Standards findings and counts. Those findings stand on their own evidence.
-
~~~~

----
-name: engineering-principles
-description: Shared decision principles for implementation, refactoring, architecture, review, debugging, verification, migration, and parallel work. Use when another engineering skill needs common judgment rules or the user names Laziness Protocol, Foundational Thinking, Redesign from First Principles, Subtract Before You Add, Minimize Reader Load, Outcome-Oriented Execution, Experience First, Exhaust the Design Space, Build the Lever, Model Behavior Structurally, Boundary Discipline, Type System Discipline, Make Operations Idempotent, Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs, Separate Before Serializing Shared State, Treat Observable Behavior as Contract, Fail Loudly, Prove It Works, Protect the Signal, Fix Root Causes, Attack the Premise, Explain the Number, Sequence Verifiable Units, Guard the Context Window, Keep Execution Unblocked, or Encode Lessons in Structure.
----
-
-# Engineering Principles
-
-A shared vocabulary for recurring engineering decisions. A principle is a default that changes a concrete choice, not a checklist item or a substitute for evidence.
-
-## Precedence
-
-Resolve conflicts in this order:
-
-1. The user's explicit product decision.
-2. The accepted spec and observable product behavior.
-3. Repository standards and ADRs.
-4. Runtime evidence.
-5. These principles as defaults.
-
-When two principles pull in different directions, preserve agreed behavior and a working feedback loop, then prefer the smaller reversible step. Surface the conflict when it materially changes the design.
-
-Scale deliberation to reversibility. A two-way door proceeds on precedent and is corrected afterwards; a one-way door, such as data loss, a published contract, or an external action, earns design exploration and confirmation.
-
-## Apply selectively
-
-1. Classify the current decision before acting: product experience, data shape, boundary, type, lifecycle, migration, verification, collaboration, or recurring lesson.
-2. Scan the index triggers against the current decision, using the request, accepted artifacts, repository, and proposed change. This scan is the agent's job; the user does not need to name a principle.
-3. Include every matched principle that could materially change the decision, normally one to four.
-4. Add every principle the user names even when the independent scan would not have selected it, then reconcile it through Precedence.
-5. Read each selected reference in full unless it is already available in the current context, then translate it into a constraint, design choice, or proof obligation before acting.
-
-Reuse the selection and references while the decision and their contents remain available in the current context. Revisit selection when a new material decision appears, not merely when another workflow starts. After compaction or a fresh context, reload only the selected references whose contents are no longer available.
-
-For delegated work, pass the relevant constraints, their rationale, and reference pointers. Each worker selects principles for its own decision surface, reusing supplied constraints that fully capture the applicable rule and reading references when it needs missing detail or additional principles. A worker does not inherit the parent's entire reading list.
-
-Do not load an unmatched reference or run the whole index as a review. Name a principle in the final report only when the user requested it, it resolved a conflict, or it drove a non-obvious decision.
-
-Selection is complete when every material decision surface has been scanned and every matching or user-named principle is applied or ruled out by its boundary.
-
-## Core
-
-- **Laziness Protocol**: sizing a diff or considering another abstraction, wrapper, parameter, layer, or dependency. Read [references/laziness-protocol.md](references/laziness-protocol.md).
-- **Foundational Thinking**: choosing core data structures, shared types, or scaffold that every later slice needs. Read [references/foundational-thinking.md](references/foundational-thinking.md).
-- **Redesign from First Principles**: integrating a new requirement that does not fit the current shape. Read [references/redesign-from-first-principles.md](references/redesign-from-first-principles.md).
-- **Subtract Before You Add**: extending or rewriting code that already carries dead or superseded paths. Read [references/subtract-before-you-add.md](references/subtract-before-you-add.md).
-- **Minimize Reader Load**: tracing requires too many layers, aliases, mutable facts, or pass-through calls. Read [references/minimize-reader-load.md](references/minimize-reader-load.md).
-- **Outcome-Oriented Execution**: an intermediate design, migration state, or compatibility path may outlive its purpose. Read [references/outcome-oriented-execution.md](references/outcome-oriented-execution.md).
-- **Experience First**: product scope or UX is being traded against implementation convenience. Read [references/experience-first.md](references/experience-first.md).
-- **Exhaust the Design Space**: a costly-to-reverse design has no strong precedent and several plausible shapes. Read [references/exhaust-the-design-space.md](references/exhaust-the-design-space.md).
-- **Build the Lever**: repeated, broad, or uncertain work can be performed or proved by a reusable tool. Read [references/build-the-lever.md](references/build-the-lever.md).
-
-## Architecture
-
-- **Model Behavior Structurally**: rules repeat as conditionals or state assumptions across the codebase. Read [references/model-behavior-structurally.md](references/model-behavior-structurally.md).
-- **Boundary Discipline**: parsing, validation, errors, or framework concerns are crossing into business logic. Read [references/boundary-discipline.md](references/boundary-discipline.md).
-- **Type System Discipline**: types permit invalid domain states or external data enters as trusted. Read [references/type-system-discipline.md](references/type-system-discipline.md).
-- **Make Operations Idempotent**: commands, jobs, migrations, or lifecycle steps may retry or resume after partial progress. Read [references/make-operations-idempotent.md](references/make-operations-idempotent.md).
-- **Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs**: an internal API is being replaced while callers still exist. Read [references/migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis.md](references/migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis.md).
-- **Separate Before Serializing Shared State**: concurrent actors may write the same branch, file, key, process, or object. Read [references/separate-before-serializing-shared-state.md](references/separate-before-serializing-shared-state.md).
-- **Treat Observable Behavior as Contract**: a change alters output, ordering, errors, timing, defaults, identifiers, or formats that outsiders can observe. Read [references/treat-observable-behavior-as-contract.md](references/treat-observable-behavior-as-contract.md).
-- **Fail Loudly**: code catches errors, calls remote dependencies, retries, falls back, or receives malformed input. Read [references/fail-loudly.md](references/fail-loudly.md).
-
-## Verification
-
-- **Prove It Works**: work is about to be called complete. Read [references/prove-it-works.md](references/prove-it-works.md).
-- **Protect the Signal**: a check fails and the tempting fix changes the check rather than the code. Read [references/protect-the-signal.md](references/protect-the-signal.md).
-- **Fix Root Causes** (including Attack the Premise): a bug, failure, or performance regression is being diagnosed, or performance is being optimized. Read [references/fix-root-causes.md](references/fix-root-causes.md).
-- **Explain the Number**: a measured result will support a performance claim or decision. Read [references/explain-the-number.md](references/explain-the-number.md).
-- **Sequence Verifiable Units**: work spans several slices, commits, tickets, or migration batches, or validation must be scoped, scheduled, or rerun. Read [references/sequence-verifiable-units.md](references/sequence-verifiable-units.md).
-
-## Collaboration
-
-- **Guard the Context Window**: a phase boundary, long investigation, large output, or parallel fan-out threatens useful context. Read [references/guard-the-context-window.md](references/guard-the-context-window.md).
-- **Keep Execution Unblocked**: a reversible choice risks an unnecessary human checkpoint, or background work is pending while independent work may remain. Read [references/keep-execution-unblocked.md](references/keep-execution-unblocked.md).
-- **Encode Lessons in Structure**: a correction or instruction has become recurring. Read [references/encode-lessons-in-structure.md](references/encode-lessons-in-structure.md).
~~~~

-# Boundary Discipline
-
-**Apply when:** external input, framework state, transport errors, or validation logic is entering business behavior.
-
-Parse and validate once where untrusted data crosses into the system: CLI arguments, configuration, network requests, storage records, environment variables, and third-party APIs. Convert it into trusted domain types there.
-
-Inside the boundary, keep business functions direct and trust the established types and invariants. Convert internal results back to framework or transport shapes at the exit boundary.
-
-Do not scatter defensive checks through every layer. Keep a guard inside only when the invariant can genuinely be broken there by concurrent state or an independently trusted subsystem.

-# Build the Lever
-
-**Apply when:** work is repeated, broad, error-prone, or uncertain enough that a reusable tool can perform or prove it.
-
-Build the smallest script, codemod, generator, fixture, checker, or driving route that turns the work into a deterministic operation. The lever should be the artifact a reviewer can run, not a private convenience whose output must be trusted.
-
-Build it before the bulk work when every later unit benefits. Keep it only when repetition, risk, or future maintenance repays its cost; otherwise use a throwaway script and remove it during cleanup.
-
-A lever does not justify automation around a one-line edit. Its value is repeatability, coverage, or stronger evidence.
~~~~

-# Encode Lessons in Structure
-
-**Apply when:** the same correction, failure mode, or instruction has appeared more than once.

-
-Use agent instructions only when the rule is judgment-dependent and cannot be represented structurally. Keep one source of truth and point to it rather than repeating the meaning across skills, standards, and repository guidance.
-

-# Exhaust the Design Space
-
-**Apply when:** a design is expensive to reverse, lacks a strong repository precedent, and admits several structurally different shapes.
-
-Produce at least two genuinely different designs or prototypes before selecting one. Whole-shape alternatives vary ownership, interface, data model, or interaction; changing a method name inside one architecture is not an alternative.
-
-For module interfaces, call the Skill tool with `codebase-design` and use its Design It Twice process. For observable state or UI questions, call the Skill tool with `prototype`. Compare alternatives by the decisions they expose, not by presentation polish.
-
-Skip this for mechanical work and decisions already settled by a strong local precedent. Exploration earns its cost only before a consequential choice closes options.
~~~~

-# Experience First
-
-**Apply when:** product scope or user experience is being traded against implementation convenience.
-
-Choose the smallest coherent experience that solves the user's problem well. Do not expose internal constraints as extra user steps, confusing modes, leaky terminology, or rough behavior merely because they make the implementation easier.
-

-

-# Explain the Number
-
-**Apply when:** a measured result will support a performance claim or a decision, including a benchmark or an evaluation.
-
-Before running, state the decision the measurement informs, the smallest effect that would change it, and the expected noise. Define successful work at the measured boundary so an error, skipped operation, or unused result cannot masquerade as an improvement.
-
-Compare equivalent inputs, outputs, and successful work under representative settings. Check the measured path actually ran. For a performance claim, identify what bounds the result from counters or a profile taken separately from the timed trials. Check whether a local speedup matters on the path the user waits for before claiming an end-to-end gain.
-
-When choosing between alternatives, interleave repeated trials to reduce drift. Report the workload, metric and unit, central result, run count, spread, and, for performance, the observed limiter. If the effect is within the run-to-run spread, report no measurable difference. If successful work, comparability, or the claimed limiter cannot be established, mark the comparison inconclusive and name the gap.
-
-For an explicitly requested ballpark, one run can suffice: confirm the work ran and succeeded, label it a single-run estimate, and do not use it to select a winner.
~~~~

</details>

@@ -1,9 +0,0 @@
-# Fail Loudly
-
-**Apply when:** code catches an error, calls a remote or slow dependency, retries, falls back to a default, or receives malformed input.
-
-Surface a failure where it happens, with the context needed to diagnose it. A catch block earns its place only by handling a named failure mode: recovering, translating at a boundary, or adding context before rethrowing. Reject malformed input with a precise error rather than guessing what the sender meant; tolerated malformation becomes an undocumented contract.
-
-Bound every failure path: a timeout on each remote call, a finite retry budget with backoff for transient errors only, and a limit on queued and concurrent work.
-
-A fallback or degraded mode is valid when the product requires it. Make it observable through a log, metric, or visible state so degradation is never mistaken for success.
~~~~

</details>

@@ -1,11 +0,0 @@
-# Fix Root Causes
-
-**Apply when:** a bug, failure, or performance regression is being diagnosed, or performance is being optimized.
-
-Reproduce the exact reported symptom before changing production code. Build a tight, red-capable feedback loop, minimise the case, form falsifiable hypotheses, and collect runtime evidence until one mechanism survives. For performance, profile before changing code, optimize the measured constraint, and re-measure because the constraint moves.
-
-Fix that mechanism at the point where the violated invariant is owned. A guard that only suppresses the exception, retry that only lowers frequency, or special case for the observed input is not a root-cause fix.
-
-**Attack the Premise:** If two attempted fixes based on the same assumption fail the same check, set the failed fixes aside. Write down the shared assumption and run a probe whose result would differ if it were false. Use the observed result to revise or narrow the hypothesis before attempting another fix.
-
-When this principle is applied outside an active diagnosis workflow, call the Skill tool with `diagnosing-bugs` for the full procedure. After the fix, call the Skill tool with `verify` against the original public path.
~~~~

</details>

-# Foundational Thinking
-
-**Apply when:** choosing core data structures, shared types, or scaffold that every later slice needs.
-
-Name the data shape before writing the logic. Trace its dominant reads, writes, invariants, ownership, and concurrent actors; choose a structure that makes those operations obvious and invalid states difficult.
-
-Build scaffold first only when every subsequent slice benefits from it: a stable shared type, a tight feedback loop, or a required verification route. Subtract obsolete structure before adding foundations.
-
-Keep the foundation narrow. Three explicit statements are cheaper than a speculative framework. Each foundational change should land as a coherent, verifiable unit that later work can rely on.
~~~~

</details>

-# Guard the Context Window
-
-**Apply when:** a phase boundary, long investigation, large output, or parallel fan-out threatens the context needed for sound judgment.
-
-Keep primary-source reasoning in the current session while the next phase still depends on it and the work fits. Delegate independent bulk reading or checks, then retain compact findings and artifact pointers rather than raw output.
-
-Move context only at a phase boundary. Use a handoff when the work must travel to another harness, directory, colleague, or forked side task; use a fresh ticket context when the ticket is self-contained.
-
-Summaries are lossy. Do not compact or hand off merely to make the window look tidy, and do not keep bulk payloads in the lead session when only their conclusions are needed.
-
-Keep check output small. Run tests and linters in their quiet modes and keep the exit status, counts, failing cases, and an artifact pointer, not coverage tables or repeated warnings. After a compaction, recover from compact notes and the files the next step touches rather than rereading everything read before.
~~~~

</details>

+++ upstream/(absent)/references/keep-execution-unblocked.md
@@ -1,11 +0,0 @@
-# Keep Execution Unblocked
-
-**Apply when:** a reversible execution choice is about to become a human checkpoint, or a background command, agent, or investigation is pending.
-
-Facts are the agent's job. Inspect the repository, run the experiment, or use the available tool instead of asking the user to supply observable information. Proceed on reversible implementation details when the accepted behavior and repository precedent make the choice clear, then present the result for asynchronous correction.
-
-Decisions are the user's job when they change product direction, scope, experience, risk acceptance, or another genuine preference. Irreversible external actions also require confirmation.
-
-A running command, agent, or investigation blocks only work that depends on its result. Continue independent implementation, documentation, or review work before waiting at a completion barrier. Preserve prerequisite ordering and serialize work that shares mutable state.
-
-Keep one owner responsible for each background job's completion and evidence. Use completion notifications when available rather than duplicate watchers or status polling. Before declaring the task complete, collect the actual terminal results of required jobs; successful submission is not successful execution.
~~~~

</details>

-# Laziness Protocol
-
-**Apply when:** sizing a diff or considering another abstraction, wrapper, option, guard, signal, layer, or dependency.
-
-Prefer deletion and the smallest change that fully satisfies the accepted behavior. Start by asking what can disappear, what the language or framework already provides, and whether an existing deep module should own the behavior. A new dependency, service, or language spends an innovation token: prefer what the stack already uses, and add one only when it removes more maintenance than it brings.
-
-A smaller diff is not automatically better. Do not omit required behavior, collapse distinct domain concepts, or hide complexity in callers to reduce line count. The target is less system, not less visible code.
-
-A new abstraction earns its place only when it hides real complexity for more than one present caller or establishes an agreed seam. Otherwise keep the direct code.
~~~~

</details>

-# Make Operations Idempotent
-
-**Apply when:** a command, job, webhook, migration, setup step, or lifecycle operation may retry or resume after partial progress.
-
-Define the intended end state, then make each run converge on it. Repeating a completed operation should preserve the same externally observable result rather than duplicate records, compound mutations, or fail because prior work exists.
-
-Use stable identities, upserts, compare-and-set transitions, checkpoints, or existence checks at the owning boundary as the domain requires. Idempotency keys and locks are tools, not the definition.
-
-Prove first run, repeated run, and recovery after an interrupted intermediate state. Do not erase a legitimate repeated user action merely because the implementation cannot distinguish it from a retry.
~~~~

</details>

@@ -1,9 +0,0 @@
-# Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs
-
-**Apply when:** an internal API is replaced while callers still exist.
-
-Prefer one verifiable wave: inventory every caller, migrate them, update tests to the new contract, prove no caller remains, and delete the old API and compatibility tests.
-
-Use expand-contract only when an atomic cutover cannot remain buildable, deployable, or operationally safe. The expansion, migration batches, and final deletion are one bounded sequence. Create the deletion ticket up front and block it on every migration batch so compatibility cannot become the accidental steady state.
-
-Preserve compatibility for external consumers only when the product or versioning contract requires it. Name that contract and its removal or support policy explicitly.
~~~~

</details>

@@ -1,9 +0,0 @@
-# Minimize Reader Load
-
-**Apply when:** answering one code question requires following many wrappers, aliases, mutable facts, or pass-through calls.
-
-Count what a maintainer must hold in their head between the question and its answer. Collapse one-caller wrappers, shorten message chains, colocate state with the behavior that owns it, and shrink mutable scope.
-
-Prefer a deep module that hides complexity behind a narrow interface. When the interface or seam itself needs redesign, call the Skill tool with `codebase-design`.
-
-Do not flatten meaningful domain distinctions or hide operationally important behavior. The aim is locality: fewer places to inspect for one change, not fewer named concepts at any cost.
~~~~

</details>

@@ -1,9 +0,0 @@
-# Model Behavior Structurally
-
-**Apply when:** the same state rule or shape assumption appears in several conditionals, files, or callers.
-
-First settle the project's domain language. When that language is changing, call the Skill tool with `domain-modeling`. Then encode state, transitions, variants, and invariants so invalid combinations are difficult or impossible to represent.
-
-The structure should make valid transitions clear and invalid states difficult to represent. Callers consume it; they do not reimplement its rules.
-
-Do not create a framework for one local branch. The repeated knowledge, not the number of lines, is the signal that a model is missing.
~~~~

-# Outcome-Oriented Execution
-
-**Apply when:** a plan introduces intermediate architecture, compatibility code, or migration states.
-
-Every intermediate state must do at least one useful job:
-
-- Deliver observable value.
-- Preserve a required migration or deployment invariant.
-- Establish verified scaffold that later work immediately consumes.
-
-Delete states that exist only to make the plan appear smooth. Do not preserve an old and new path without an explicit reason and removal condition.
-
-Tracer bullets are valid intermediate states because each is independently useful and verifiable. Expand-contract is valid when an atomic cutover cannot stay safe; its contract step and deletion ticket must already be part of the sequence.
~~~~

+++ upstream/(absent)/references/protect-the-signal.md
@@ -1,9 +0,0 @@
-# Protect the Signal
-
-**Apply when:** a test, type check, lint rule, assertion, threshold, or other check fails and the tempting fix changes the check rather than the code.
-
-A check is evidence only while it can fail. Fix the code that violates it. Skipping or deleting a test, loosening an assertion, special-casing the test input, adding a suppression or cast, or raising a threshold turns the check green without making the claim true.
-
-Change a check only when the check itself is wrong: it asserts obsolete behavior, pins an implementation detail, or observes nondeterministically. State that reason in the diff or report, and keep or replace the coverage it provided.
-
-The same holds for delegated work. When inspecting another agent's diff, treat every weakened check as a claim to verify.
~~~~

</details>

@@ -1,11 +0,0 @@
-# Prove It Works
-
-**Apply when:** work is about to be called complete.
-
-Identify the observable claim, then check the real artifact directly. Run the public path, read the actual value, inspect the produced file or diff, and verify the full input-to-output chain. Compilation, tests, cached representations, and agent reports are supporting signals rather than substitutes for the claimed result.
-
-Choose the least expensive evidence sufficient for the observable claim and repository requirements. Broader checks earn their cost by covering additional relevant failure modes.
-
-For user-facing application behavior, call the Skill tool with `verify`. Its `VERIFIED`, `NOT VERIFIED`, and `INCONCLUSIVE` verdicts preserve the evidence boundary.
-
-Inspect delegated changes and validate their integration yourself. Reuse recorded checks whose scope and inputs remain valid; repeat them when integration changes those inputs or the evidence is insufficient. Apply Sequence Verifiable Units to check validity and required fresh evidence. A worker's completion report alone is not proof. When a check passes too easily, test the observation method before concluding the system is correct.
~~~~

-# Redesign from First Principles
-
-**Apply when:** a new requirement repeatedly fights the current shape.
-
-Redesign as if the requirement had been a day-one assumption. Reconsider ownership, data shape, interfaces, and lifecycle instead of attaching another conditional or adapter at the point where the symptom appears.
-
-Preserve accepted behavior, not accidental structure. Ground the redesign in current callers, recorded decisions, and runtime evidence. If the design is costly to reverse and lacks precedent, apply Exhaust the Design Space before committing.
-
-One awkward edge case is not evidence that the architecture is wrong. Redesign when the same workaround or escape hatch appears across independent parts of the implementation.
~~~~

@@ -1,9 +0,0 @@
-# Separate Before Serializing Shared State
-
-**Apply when:** concurrent actors may write the same file, branch, key, process, database row, or in-memory object.
-
-First remove unnecessary sharing. Give workers separate worktrees, branches, output paths, ports, profiles, fixtures, partitions, or immutable inputs. Aggregate completed artifacts through one explicit owner.
-
-Serialize only when one shared writer is a real invariant of the domain. Put that ownership in the structure rather than relying on timing, politeness, retries, or an undocumented lock order.
-
-Before parallelizing, name every shared mutable resource and how it is isolated or owned. If that cannot be stated, the workstreams are not independent yet.
~~~~

</details>

<summary><code>references/sequence-verifiable-units.md</code>: absent upstream</summary>


~~~~diff
--- local/skills/engineering-principles/references/sequence-verifiable-units.md
+++ upstream/(absent)/references/sequence-verifiable-units.md
@@ -1,15 +0,0 @@
-# Sequence Verifiable Units
-
-**Apply when:** work spans several slices, commits, tickets, or migration batches, or validation must be scoped, scheduled, or rerun.
-
-Break the work into the smallest units that each end in a meaningful check. Order prerequisite scaffold and risky unknowns before dependent behavior. Verify and integrate one unit before starting dependent work so a failure has a narrow search space; finished work on a side branch is not progress. Make the change easy, then make the easy change: land behavior-preserving restructuring as its own unit, proved unchanged by existing checks, before the behavior change that needs it.
-
-Within a unit, use focused checks to answer implementation questions. Run the required final validation once the relevant implementation and generated artifacts stabilize; a focused result does not replace broader coverage. Schedule independent checks together when their resource and mutable-state requirements permit it. Repository instructions own the required commands and evidence; run a separate build only for a required build path not already exercised by those checks.
-
-When a broad check reveals a shared failure that makes further results uninformative, stop the run and diagnose with focused checks. Resume required broader coverage after fixing the shared cause.
-
-A successful check stands while its scope, relevant source, dependencies, generated artifacts, configuration, toolchain, and execution environment remain unchanged. Record the command and scope; rerun checks whose results a later change could affect. Reuse normal caches where permitted by repository policy, and require fresh execution when external state, nondeterminism, or an explicit evidence contract demands it. A cached result cannot substitute for required fresh race, integration, or live evidence.
-
-For product work, prefer tracer bullets that deliver a complete public path through the necessary layers. For migrations that cannot be atomic, keep each expand-contract batch buildable and reserve a final unit for deleting the old path.
-
-The sequence should tell the engineering story: baseline or failing reproduction, enabling structure, behavior, cleanup, and final real-surface proof.
~~~~

</details>

-# Subtract Before You Add
-
-**Apply when:** extending or rewriting code that already carries dead, duplicated, superseded, or transitional paths.
-
-Remove what the new behavior makes obsolete before building on top. Delete dead adapters, redundant validation, stale branches, abandoned scaffolding, and tests that protect only obsolete implementation details.
-
-Prove each deletion is safe through references and executable behavior. Do not combine unrelated cleanup with the requested change merely because it is nearby.
-
-The result should expose the real remaining design. Adding to a simplified base is safer than teaching new code to coexist with weight that no longer has an owner.
~~~~

-# Treat Observable Behavior as Contract
-
-**Apply when:** a change alters output, ordering, error shape or text, timing, defaults, identifiers, or a file or wire format that anything outside the changed module can observe.
-
-With enough consumers, every observable behavior is depended on by somebody, whether or not it was promised. Before changing, inventory what becomes visibly different at the public surface, including behavior the documentation never mentions.
-
-Classify each difference as intended, incidental, or a break. Keep incidental behavior stable when changing it buys nothing. When a break is intended, name it in the PR, changelog, or migration note, and move internal callers with Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs.
-
-Do not freeze implementation detail that nothing outside the module can reach. Behavior visible only to the module's own tests is not a contract; rewrite those tests against the public behavior.
~~~~

@@ -1,9 +0,0 @@
-# Type System Discipline
-
-**Apply when:** a signature or model permits invalid domain states, semantic primitives are interchangeable, or external data enters as trusted.
-
-Make illegal states unrepresentable where the language permits it. Use distinct variants for distinct states, semantic types for identifiers and units that must not mix, and exhaustive handling for closed sets.
-
-Parse external values at a boundary before treating them as domain data. Derive types from the authoritative schema when one exists. Prefer narrowing and construction functions over casts, unchecked assertions, optional fields that are always required in practice, or escape hatches such as `any`.
-
-Do not add type machinery that makes ordinary valid states harder to express. The type should remove caller knowledge, not move runtime confusion into generic syntax.
~~~~

~~~~diff
--- local/skills/formal-verify/SKILL.md
+++ upstream/(absent)/SKILL.md
@@ -1,41 +0,0 @@
----
-name: formal-verify
-description: Create, run, or maintain formal verification of a named property in a model or actual code. Use when the user requests model checking, a formal proof, or an audit of formal verification, or when an existing project formal check is required for the change.
----
-
-# Formal verify
-
-Check a **property** over a stated scope: every reachable state or event order in a model, every input in a code verifier's domain, or the domain of a proof. This complements `verify`, which observes behavior on the real shipped surface. Neither supplies the other's evidence.
-
-## Route
-
-Inspect `docs/agents/formal-verification/`, then choose one branch:
-
-- **Create**: the user asks for a reusable formal check. Read [references/create.md](references/create.md) and [references/project-format.md](references/project-format.md).
-- **Run**: the user asks to check a property, or a project formal obligation applies. Read [references/run.md](references/run.md). The project record owns the command for an existing check.
-- **Maintain**: the user asks to audit, update, or repair existing checks. Read [references/maintain.md](references/maintain.md) and [references/project-format.md](references/project-format.md).
-
-Maintain with no artifact routes to Create. Create with an existing artifact routes to Maintain unless the user explicitly requests replacement or a new check. Run with no artifact performs the strongest direct or scratch check available and reports the missing reusable route. Run leaves no permanent project files.
-
-## Proof standard
-
-- State the property from the intended promise, not from the implementation expression that decides it. Check that a success path and any property antecedent are reachable; a vacuous pass is not evidence for the promise.
-- Name the checked target, tool, bounds, assumptions (including fairness where relevant), reductions, and exclusions. Claim completion only for the properties the checker actually evaluated. For an unbounded claim, cite a proof or completed analysis that covers the unbounded dimension; a bounded pass does not establish it.
-- Keep model and code claims separate. Use a verifier that analyzes the actual implementation for a proof about the code itself. To apply a detached model's result to the code's event orders, establish that its actions, guards, and atomicity match the actual source revision. A stale model can still be checked as a model. Replay a counterexample against real code step by step before calling it a product bug. State a replay gap when correspondence of the trace is unknown.
-- Create and Maintain demonstrate sensitivity in the checked target: break a detached model with a faulty transition, or break the implementation analyzed by a code verifier in scratch. A detached model's negative control shows model sensitivity, not that the checker can catch a source-only mutation. See [references/sensitivity.md](references/sensitivity.md) for the procedure.
-
-## Verdicts
-
-Report one verdict per requested formal property, qualified by its target and scope:
-
-- **VERIFIED**: the prescribed formal check completed and the property held within the stated scope.
-- **NOT VERIFIED**: the check found a counterexample to the named property on the stated target.
-- **INCONCLUSIVE**: the tool, check completion, or a premise needed for the claim could not be established. A model-only finding does not resolve a current-code claim with unproven correspondence.
-
-Report the exact command, the observed result, and evidence locations. Preserve raw checker output and any trace with secrets and private data redacted before sharing. Report generated-input tests separately as test evidence, never as a formal verdict.
-
-## Ownership boundary
-
-Create and Maintain edit only the verification artifact and the models, harnesses, or helpers it owns. A product bug is a finding, not a reason to redefine the property or change product code during formal verification.
-
-If the user requests a chart for a checked transition model, call the Skill tool with `statechart`. Pass the exact model and configuration used for the check, the checked revision, and the raw checker evidence. The chart is a view of that check, not another proof or a condition for a verdict.
~~~~

</details>

<details>
<summary><code>references/create.md</code>: absent upstream</summary>


~~~~diff
--- local/skills/formal-verify/references/create.md
+++ upstream/(absent)/references/create.md
@@ -1,36 +0,0 @@
-# Create project formal verification
-
-A test checks the cases that someone thought to write. Formal verification checks every case in a stated scope. Find the part of the repo where that matters most, verify one property of it, and leave a project-local record that lets the next agent check a change against that property. Write for an agent who reads it cold, mid-change, and has never seen your work. The user must be able to trust the result and act on it without learning the verification language.
-
-## Choose the target from the code
-
-Answer from the codebase, and ask the user only what you cannot observe. If the user named an area or a bug, start there.
-
-A good target is a promise the code makes, where a break harms users and tests rarely reach the case that breaks it. Choose the strongest such target in the repo, not the one that is easiest to verify. State the property and harm in one plain sentence each, then say which success path and preconditions must be reachable before choosing a tool.
-
-## Let the question choose the tool
-
-Use [tool-choice.md](tool-choice.md) to select the least costly tool that answers the question. Prefer a suitable existing checker. If only generated-input tests are possible, report the tool gap and the test result separately; do not publish a formal record for a test-only check.
-
-## What makes it good
-
-- **True to the code.** Every part of a code-facing model or proof points to code that a reviewer can open. What the verification treats as one indivisible step is one indivisible step in the code. Names come from this repo. Label a design-only model as such.
-- **Able to fail.** Show each property failing on a deliberately broken variant of the target it checks, as described in [sensitivity.md](sensitivity.md).
-- **Findings stay findings.** When the current code breaks the property, report it with the counterexample in the code's terms. Keep the property and product code as they are.
-- **Honest about scope.** Say what is verified, under which bounds and assumptions, and what is left out. A pass covers the model or the bound, not the whole system.
-- **Readable without the tool.** Tell a counterexample as a short sequence of steps in the code's words.
-- **Cheap to rerun.** One command, a reproducible tool version, and a run short enough that the next agent will use it on a relevant change.
-- **Kept in step with the code.** Record which files and functions each check covers, and the commit at which you last confirmed that the verification describes them.
-
-## Write the project record
-
-Use [project-format.md](project-format.md). From the record alone, the next agent must be able to tell whether a change touches the verified code, run the check, tell a real bug from a modeling error, and update the verification when a change is intended. Use this repo's real commands, paths, and nouns, and leave no placeholders.
-
-## Prove it before you hand off
-
-Follow the record as the next agent would. Run the baseline at the intended revision, observe the success path and antecedent, and capture the result. Perform the documented negative control in isolation, remove the break, and rerun the baseline. The result must be back where it started: passing, or failing only on the findings you will report. If the record misses the break or a step does not run, fix the record or the verification, not the scratch change. A record whose command and sensitivity have not been demonstrated is still unproven; report the gap.
-
-## Hand off
-
-Tell the user what you verified, which tool you used and why, the bounds, what the check found in plain words, how to run it, and what it does not cover. Include the baseline, sensitivity evidence, and restored result. Suggest a second target only if you found a close one. Point the user at Maintain for bringing the verification back in line after changes that did not recheck it.
-
~~~~

</details>

<details>
<summary><code>references/maintain.md</code>: absent upstream</summary>


~~~~diff
--- local/skills/formal-verify/references/maintain.md
+++ upstream/(absent)/references/maintain.md
@@ -1,47 +0,0 @@
-# Maintain project formal verification
-
-A formal check proves a property of what it describes. When the code changes and the verification does not, the check can keep passing while it describes code that no longer exists. That pass is the dangerous case, because it looks like a proof. This workflow handles the changes that skipped the check: merges, edits made without the project record, and drift that builds up across many commits.
-
-## Outcomes
-
-Report correspondence and the property verdict separately. Give each check an alignment outcome:
-
-- **in sync**: no change since the last sync alters what the check describes.
-- **updated**: the source or design changed, and the verification now describes it.
-- **blocked**: correspondence or the required recheck could not be established. Say exactly why.
-
-An in-sync or updated check can expose a **bug**: the verification describes the current code, and the code breaks the property. This is a finding about the code. It is not drift.
-
-## Edit scope
-
-Edit only the verification: project records, models, harnesses, and property files it owns. When a property fails on the current code, keep the property as stated and report the failure. Keep verification changes separate from any product fix.
-
-## Pass
-
-For a design-only check, compare against the accepted design and track the checked model version instead of a source commit. Its counterexamples are design findings, not product bugs.
-
-1. **Find the checks.** Read `docs/agents/formal-verification/README.md` and every check record in scope, or the one the user named. Collect the property, the code it covers, the bounds and assumptions, the command that runs it, and the commit where it was last confirmed to describe the code. If no artifact exists, route to Create. If the record has no sync commit, use the last commit that changed the verification files as a starting point for review; say that you did and do not treat it as evidence of alignment.
-2. **Run it as it is.** Run each check once before you change anything, and record the result. A pass here does not tell you that the code is correct. It tells you that the old description still holds. A failure here can be drift or a bug. Do not decide which until step 5.
-3. **Read every change to covered code.** Diff the covered files from the sync commit to the current revision, including local edits in scope, and read each commit message. Also look for code that moved: a covered function that is renamed, split, or moved to another file is still covered code. Also look for new code that touches the state that a check guards, such as a new function that writes the same fields. For each change, decide which of these it is:
-   - **No effect.** The change does not alter anything the verification describes, such as formatting, comments, or code paths that the verification does not cover. Check this against the model or harness, not against the commit message.
-   - **The verification no longer describes the code.** A step that was one indivisible action is now two, a branch was added or removed, a check moved, a new path reaches the guarded state, or a value now has a different range. The model or harness must change.
-   - **The promise changed on purpose.** The change alters what the code promises, and evidence in the change says that this is intended: the doc comment, the tests, the changelog, or the commit message. The property must change, and you must cite that evidence.
-   - **The promise may be broken.** The code changed, and no evidence says that the promise changed. Treat a failure that follows as a bug candidate.
-4. **Update from the code, not from the result.** Change the model or harness so that each changed part again points to code that a reviewer can open, and keep one indivisible step in the code as one step in the verification. Write the update from the code before you rerun, and do not shape it by what makes the check pass. Change a property only for a promise that changed on purpose. Write down the old wording, the new wording, and the evidence. Keep the bounds unless the change makes them wrong. If you must reduce a bound, say so in the report.
-5. **Rerun and judge each result.** Run each affected check using the revised record. Reestablish reachability and re-prove each affected negative control in scratch using [sensitivity.md](sensitivity.md), then remove the break and restore the baseline.
-   - **Pass:** report what actually held. A passing stale model is not evidence about current code.
-   - **Fail:** replay the counterexample against the real code, step by step. If a step is impossible, fix the verification and say what was wrong. If every step is established, report the bug and the harm in the code's own words. Include the introducing commit if established and a cheap real-code reproduction if available. If correspondence of the trace is unresolved, report a model finding and the replay gap rather than a product bug.
-6. **Update the project record.** Update the covered code, action-to-source mapping, commands, bounds, and assumptions. Follow the finalized record as the next agent would and report any step you could not run. Move the sync commit only to a source commit confirmed to match, including when an aligned check exposes a bug. Do not move it for a blocked check or to stand for uncommitted changes.
-
-## Report
-
-Tell the user, for each check:
-
-- the alignment outcome, the property verdict, and the commits that you read;
-- what changed in the verification and why, citing the evidence if the promise changed on purpose;
-- the rerun result and the break that showed the updated check can still fail;
-- each established bug: the counterexample as steps in the code's words, the harm, and the introducing commit if known;
-- what the verification still does not cover, including new code that it should cover and does not.
-
-Say outright which failures were drift in the verification and which were bugs in the code. For a check that passed before you updated it and fails after, say that the old pass was on a stale description.
-
~~~~

</details>

-# Project formal verification format
-
-The artifact is portable agent-facing documentation, not a harness-specific installed skill. The unit of coverage is an independently runnable check, not a user-facing feature.
-
-## Layout
-
-`docs/agents/formal-verification/README.md` indexes one `<check>.md` record per independently runnable check. Give each entry a plain-language property and a routing cue for which areas or changes should use it. Keep models, proof files, harnesses, and scripts in established project locations and link them from the record. Keep real-surface driving instructions in their own artifact.
-
-## Check record
-
-Use these sections in each record:
-
-- **Property**: the promise, the harm if broken, and the success path and any antecedent that must be reachable. If one command checks several named properties, identify each separately.
-- **Target and coverage**: a detached model, a design-only model, or a verifier analyzing real code. Name the covered files, symbols, entry points, and state writers. Where a model represents code, map its actions, guards, and atomicity to source. Where a tool analyzes code, identify the entry point, harness, and any stubs or abstractions.
-- **Run**: one exact command, its working directory, tool and version, prerequisites, and the configuration or proof files it uses. Explain the expected success, violation, and incomplete-run signals so an agent can distinguish a failing property from a broken command.
-- **Scope**: constants, bounds, inputs, environment assumptions, fairness, reductions, and excluded cases as applicable. For an unbounded claim, identify what actually discharges it.
-- **Negative control**: the reversible change and commands needed to produce a violation in isolation, its expected diagnostic or distinguishing trace, and the baseline to restore. State whether it demonstrates model or code-verifier sensitivity and name any independent implementation replay.
-- **Last aligned revision**: the source commit confirmed to match the record, not merely the last commit on which a checker ran. Design-only artifacts name the model version and state that no code correspondence is claimed. Keep this separate from the last property verdict.
-
-Write exact repository instructions, not generic examples or placeholders. A future agent must be able to tell whether a change touches the check and run the recorded command cold.
-
-## Evidence
-
-Put commands, status, raw checker output, traces, and control results in run-owned evidence outside cleanup-owned scratch and the project tree. Link the evidence from the report. Keep the actual checked scope visible even when a shortened trace or chart is shown; redact secrets and private data before sharing.
~~~~

-# Run project formal verification
-
-## 1. Name the property and find the route
-
-State the promise, its target (a design model or actual code), the harm if it fails, and the requested scope. Use the user's wording and the project contract to choose the property, not whichever existing check passes. Read `docs/agents/formal-verification/README.md` and only the matching records.
-

-
-**Done when:** each requested property has a selected command or a concrete reason no formal check can run.
-
-## 2. Establish the target and revision
-
-Identify what will be checked: the actual code revision under review (identify any relevant local changes), or the exact model and configuration. Confirm what the command and harness actually analyze. For code claims backed by a detached model, compare relevant source and configuration against the last aligned commit, including moved code and new writers. Establish that actions, guards, and atomicity still correspond. If correspondence cannot be established, report the gap and label any completed run as model-only evidence. Leave drift repair to Maintain.
-

-
-## 3. Execute and capture
-
-Run the recorded command with its tool version and configuration. Isolate checker-generated files and scratch inputs outside the project tree. Capture the command, tool output, exit status, actual bounds and assumptions, reachability evidence, and any counterexample. Inspect which properties the checker completed; a timeout, unsupported check, or early exit cannot establish properties that were not checked.
-
-For a counterexample, tell the sequence in the code's or design's words. For a code claim, replay it against the real implementation one step at a time. Include a cheap reproduction if feasible, and distinguish an impossible step (verification drift) from an unconfirmed step (replay gap). Preserve a liveness loop when one is part of the counterexample.
-
-**Done when:** each requested property has raw evidence or a named observation gap, and no model-only trace is called a product bug.
-
-## 4. Clean up and report
-

Report exactly one verdict per requested formal property using the skill's verdicts. Include the command, target and revision or model/configuration, scope, observed result, evidence, and gaps. Report generated-input results as tests; if they were the only evidence for a requested formal claim, the formal claim remains `INCONCLUSIVE`.
-
-**Done when:** evidence remains accessible and no permanent project files or run-owned residue were left behind.

-# Show that the check can fail
-
-Use an isolated scratch copy of the target at the checked revision. Keep the command, property, and configuration the same so the deliberate break is the difference.
-
-- **Detached model:** inject the corresponding faulty transition in the model, such as skipping a guard or splitting an indivisible step to admit the bad order. Observe the named property fail and label it **model sensitivity**. A source-only mutation cannot change a detached model's result. Where feasible, independently replay the same schedule on the real implementation and record that evidence separately.
-- **Code verifier:** mutate the actual implementation the verifier analyzes, such as removing a guard or reordering two steps. Observe the named property fail in the real-code verifier, not in a substitute model or test.
-
-A parse error, timeout, or failure of a different property does not count. If the baseline already finds a violation, show a distinct witness attributable to the injected break; repeating the baseline finding does not establish sensitivity to the break. If the control cannot distinguish them, report the gap.
-
-Discard the mutation, rerun the baseline, and preserve both results. Confirm that the success path and any property antecedent are reachable on the baseline: a negative control does not by itself rule out a vacuous pass on the original model or code.

-# Let the question choose the tool
-
-Pick the tool that answers the question at the lowest cost: a model checker, a proof assistant, an SMT-backed verifier, or another tool. Reuse a repository checker when it answers the question.
-
-- Whether events can happen in a bad order usually suits a model checker over a small model of the design. Default to TLA+ with TLC for bounded state and event-order questions, regardless of the implementation language. Use the actual interleaving boundaries; do not model a real race as one atomic step.
-- Whether the code itself behaves for every input in a stated domain, as with overflow or a data-structure invariant, calls for a verifier that analyzes the actual implementation. A hand model of the function does not establish that claim. If no suitable verifier runs on the code, say so and test the real code with generated inputs. Report that as test evidence only.
-- If the property must hold at every size, or another dimension cannot be bounded, choose a proof method or analysis that covers that dimension and capture evidence that it completed. A finite-domain search alone does not prove a claim over all sizes.
-
-Prefer a tool that the repo's developers can install and run. Tell the user why it fits the question and what it cannot establish.
