-# Time audit
-
-Run the full measured-time branch of [retro](../SKILL.md) for the selected scope. Use **accounted time** throughout: every duration has a source, a timing basis, and an explicit treatment of overlap.
-
-## 1. Establish coverage
-
-Discover persisted sessions and their schema through the selected harness's available history/export facilities, AgentTrace discovery, or documented session storage. Read the relevant interface documentation first; derive locations from discovery rather than assuming a path or requiring an archive API. When the selected source is omp, also read [omp.md](omp.md) for its archive and event guidance.
-
-When AgentTrace is installed, read [agenttrace.md](agenttrace.md) and use its source-scoped discovery, inventory, and triage recipes alongside available native evidence. Check the installed version and help first. Reconcile inventories; AgentTrace summaries do not replace raw timing evidence or establish complete subagent coverage. If unavailable or unsupported for the selected harness, continue from accessible native records without installing dependencies and report coverage limits.
-
-Use the scope selected in retro. For a historical audit, record exact interval boundaries and timezone, anchoring the default trailing 90 days at audit start. For a specified session, include its related subagents without adding unrelated history. Identify the repo by recorded workspace metadata and canonical paths. Follow parent/child links, including worktree or temporary-directory sessions belonging to the same task. Label ambiguous repo attribution separately.
-
-Inventory sessions and events intersecting the interval, including sessions that began earlier. Record accessible dates, parent and child counts, unavailable or truncated sessions, unresolved child links, schema differences, and missing timing fields. Retain source locators so findings can cite session IDs, tool-call IDs, and event timestamps without exposing secrets.
-
-**Done when:** the report can state what portion of the requested interval and session graph was actually accessible. If history is unavailable, report the discovery attempts and missing prerequisite; draw conclusions only from accessible evidence.
-
-## 2. Account for every tool call
-
-Build one record per `(session ID, tool-call ID)`, merging duplicate or streamed events. Keep calls without IDs in a separately counted, explicitly uncertain bucket. Retain tool name, command and working directory where applicable, parent/job links, timing fields, outcome, and source locator.
-
-Use one reproducible accounting procedure for all report views. Before recomputing, apply [analysis reuse](diagnosis.md#reuse-reproducible-analysis): source fingerprints, exact window, and method determine whether an existing artifact is reusable. Record the input manifest and procedure so repeated analysis of the same snapshots yields the same ledger.
-
-For each call:
-
-- Prefer recorded execution start/end timestamps: label their difference **execution time**.
-- Otherwise use tool-result timestamp minus tool-call timestamp: label it **elapsed latency**, which can include approval, queueing, transport, and execution.
-- Separate queueing and approval delays only where recorded phase boundaries support it. Mark missing, negative, inconsistent, and unmatched intervals as unavailable rather than zero; report counts by cause.
-- Clip intervals to the audit window. Cap each individual measured wait at 15 minutes, recording the uncapped value where known and the number capped. Apply the cap consistently to the reported aggregates and retain uncapped totals separately so truncation is visible. Open waits with no end remain missing, not invented 15-minute measurements.
-- An asynchronous submission measures submission only. Link the job's recorded execution and completion events to measure its runtime once; keep polling/wait overhead separate. Identify nested tool and shell-wrapper records that describe the same execution so they are not counted twice.
-
-Maintain separate execution-time and elapsed-latency aggregates. Summed durations are **call-time**, not wall-clock time. Compute occupied wall-clock time by interval union across overlapping calls, including parent/subagent overlap; report the timing basis for each union. Overlap across categories means their occupied times need not add to the overall union. Unrecorded gaps are not measured agent thinking time.
-
-**Done when:** every discovered call has one accounted record or an explicit exclusion/missing-data reason, and async jobs, duplicate records, caps, and overlap are reconciled.
-
-## 3. Classify shell work
-
-Group shell calls by what they actually run: **typecheck, tests, build, lint, install, git, sleep, other**. Resolve wrappers and package scripts from repo files where available; flag current definitions that cannot establish historical behavior. Preserve command variants and working directories for diagnosis.
-
-Split compound commands only when timings exist for their components. Otherwise keep the whole call once in `other`, label it compound, and list its components. Classify wrapper intent rather than charging the same duration to every command it contains.
-
-For every category show hours of call-time, call count, timed count, median, and p90, separately by timing basis. State percentile convention and cap policy. Show queueing/approval totals separately where measurable. Include non-shell tools in the overall ranking so a shell-only view cannot hide the largest sink.
-
-Inspect frequency and duration together, including the largest calls and distribution clusters. Rank actual command variants as well as broad categories. Treat tool-generated health scores, recommendations, and estimated savings as triage hypotheses until checked against the ledger.
-
-**Done when:** category counts reconcile to shell-call records, missing timings stay visible, and the report distinguishes cumulative call-time from occupied wall-clock time.
-
-## 4. Trace instruction costs
-
-Inspect the selected harness's active instructions, relevant skills, and repo rules for requirements that trigger slow or redundant commands. Use the active context and available discovery facilities to locate them. Read referenced rules when their branch applies.
-
-For each implicated rule, quote the exact text with its source locator and connect it to observed session/tool-call IDs, command variants, frequency, and accounted time. Distinguish required checks from discretionary repeats and legitimate verification. Current instructions demonstrate current policy; attribute historical calls to a rule only when session evidence or a historical version supports that connection. Label other connections as hypotheses.
-
-**Done when:** each claimed instruction cost has both an exact rule citation and observed calls, with uncertainty about historical applicability stated.
-
-## 5. Diagnose and benchmark the top three sinks
-
-Rank sinks by accounted call-time, showing execution and elapsed-latency contributions separately and explaining any uncertainty that could change the ranking. Select three distinct sinks, or all available if fewer than three are supported.
-
-For each sink, read the applicable branches of [diagnosis.md](diagnosis.md). Inspect the actual command, workload, repetition pattern, and available phase timings. Measure why it is slow instead of inferring the cause from its name. Propose the cheapest fix that preserves the required behavior. Supported dependency edges may identify a blocking critical path; parentage and timestamps alone cannot.
-
-Where safe on this machine, benchmark the current command against a non-mutating alternative using [paired command benchmarks](diagnosis.md#paired-command-benchmarks). If measurement is unsafe or unavailable, report the historical baseline, any safe local baseline, and an executable experiment plan with its equivalence criterion. Claim an improvement only after measuring it.
-
-**Done when:** each selected sink has a measured baseline or explicit measurement gap, evidence for its cause, the cheapest proposed fix, and either a paired benchmark with equivalence evidence or an executable experiment plan. Name suspected causes that the measurements exonerate, especially quality gates that are not the bottleneck; preserve their required behavior.
-
-## Report
-
-Deliver:
-
-1. **Coverage and method:** interval, session/subagent coverage, missing data, timing basis, deduplication, percentile method, cap count and effect, async treatment, and overlap accounting.
-2. **Time ledger:** shell-category table and overall sink ranking, with execution time, elapsed latency, and occupied wall-clock time clearly distinguished.
-3. **Instruction costs:** exact rule citations linked to observed calls, separating supported attribution from hypotheses.
-4. **Top three sinks:** cause evidence, baseline, alternative, benchmark conditions and equivalence results, cheapest fix, and remaining experiment where needed. Use retro's candidate format and the action classification and confidence criteria in [diagnosis.md](diagnosis.md#comparable-experiments-and-proposed-actions).
-
-Return these findings to retro's presentation step. [credits.md](credits.md) records upstream techniques and deliberate departures.

-# Issue tracker: Beads
-
-Issues and specs for this repo live in its repo-local [Beads](https://github.com/steveyegge/beads) database. Use the `bd` CLI for all operations.
-
-## Conventions
-
-- **Create an issue**: `bd create "<title>" --body-file -`. Pipe or use a heredoc for a multi-line body; add `--type`, `--labels`, or `--parent` as needed.
-- **Read an issue**: `bd show <id> --json`, then `bd comments <id> --json` for its conversation history.
-- **List issues**: `bd list --status open --json` with appropriate `--label`, `--type`, or `--parent` filters.
-- **Comment on an issue**: `bd comment <id> "..."`
-- **Apply / remove labels**: `bd label add <id> "..."` / `bd label remove <id> "..."`
-- **Claim**: `bd update <id> --claim`
-- **Close**: `bd close <id> --reason "..."`
-
-Run commands from the repo so `bd` discovers the right database. Treat Beads IDs as opaque strings; don't assume they are numeric. If the repo is not initialized, ask before running `bd init`.
-
-## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"
-
-Create a Beads issue with `bd create`.
-
-## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"
-
-Run `bd show <id> --json` and `bd comments <id> --json`.
-
-## Wayfinding operations
-
-Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is an epic bead with **child** beads as tickets.
-
-- **Map**: an epic labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. Create it with `bd create "<title>" --type epic --labels wayfinder:map --body-file -`.
-- **Child ticket**: a task created with `bd create "<question>" --type task --parent <map> --no-inherit-labels --labels wayfinder:<type> --body-file -`, where `<type>` is `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, or `task`.
-- **Blocking**: Beads' native dependency edge. `bd dep add <child> <blocker>` means the child is blocked by the blocker. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
-- **Frontier query**: `bd ready --parent <map> --unassigned --sort oldest --json` lists the open, unblocked, unclaimed children in creation order.
-- **Claim**: `bd update <id> --claim`, the session's first write.
-- **Resolve**: `bd comment <id> "<answer>"`, then `bd close <id>`, then add the context pointer (gist + ticket ID) to the map with `bd comment <map> "<pointer>"`.
~~~~

-## Proof obligation
-
-Before each new test, name:
-
-- **Contract:** the observable behavior or invariant protected.
-- **Regression:** a plausible production defect that would make it fail.
-- **Gap:** why existing tests would miss that defect.
-
-Extend an existing case or table when it owns the same contract. Another layer earns a test only for a distinct boundary risk, such as serialization, persistence, or lifecycle.
-
-Test at the agreed seam using production paths. If proof requires a test-only export, getter, flag, or wrapper, reconsider the seam first.
-
 ## Anti-patterns

 - **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
 - **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
-- **Manufactured proof:** the mock or fixture supplies the behavior the assertion claims production provides. Fixtures supply inputs and boundary responses; production must produce the asserted outcome.
 - **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

 ## Rules of the loop

-- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first and observe it fail because the named behavior is missing or broken, rather than an unrelated setup, import, or type error. Then write only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
+- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
 - **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
 - **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.
~~~~

-# Chief of staff
-
-Run a long-lived coordination session. **Delegate** authorized work to fresh subagents and **remember** what they learned in a dated wiki.
+You are a chief of staff. Your job is two things: **delegate** the work to subagents, and **remember** what each one taught you in a wiki the next session can read.

 ## Delegate

-Keep questions, interviews, and check-ins in the main session. -### Procedures that need the user
+When it reports back, relay the result to the user: lead with the outcome and anything they must decide, and add detail only when it changes what they would do.

-- **Retrospective:** Sample about one in five worker sessions, including those dispatched by an implementation run. Prioritize sessions with observed friction. Offer `/retro <session reference>` for the selected session. Use its evidence to recommend which proposals to pursue; implement only the proposals the user approves.
-- **Large chunks of work:** Recommend `/to-spec` to capture the agreed scope, `/to-tickets` to publish independently verifiable slices, and `/implement-spec` to build them. These commands are user-invoked. Keep coordination in this session when the user brings back a published spec, tickets, or implementation results. Do not publish or start the build on their behalf without authorization.
+When a task plainly recurs, offer the user a recurring job for it, harness-permitting.
+
+### Procedures
+
+Some procedures you delegate live in other skills, installed beside this one. To run one, read its `SKILL.md` at the path below, relative to this skill's directory, and follow it.
+
+- **Retro** (`../retro/SKILL.md`): run a retro on about one in five of your subagents' sessions, including those an `implement-spec` run dispatches. Pick first the ones where something went wrong. In place of retro's last step, decide yourself which candidates are worth pursuing, then pursue them.
+- **Large chunks of work**: write a spec with `../to-spec/SKILL.md`, break it into tickets with `../to-tickets/SKILL.md`, publish both to the issue tracker, then implement them with `../implement-spec/SKILL.md`.

 ## Remember

-Use an existing shared wiki if one is available, following its conventions. Otherwise agree on a location before the first write. Keep an `index.md` with a link and a one-line summary per page. Give each page one subject, link related pages, and cite sources instead of copying or editing them.
+Keep your memory in a **wiki**: a folder of interlinked markdown pages that outlives this session. Knowledge that lives only in your context is lost at compaction; the wiki is how it reaches the next session. Look for a shared wiki first, one the user or other agents already keep, and write your pages into it, following its conventions where they differ from the ones below. Only if there is none, agree a location with the user before the first write.

-- **Ingest:** When you learn a durable decision, correction, or finding, update every affected page and the index.
-- **Query:** Read the index and relevant pages before making a decision or briefing a worker. File new findings worth keeping.
-- **Lint:** Periodically delegate a read-only pass for contradictions, orphan pages, broken links, and superseded claims.
+- `index.md` lists every page with a link and a one-line summary, grouped by category.
+- Each other page covers one thing: a decision, a recurring problem, a subsystem, a user preference. Link related pages to each other.
+- Sources (issues, PRs, transcripts, subagent reports) are never copied in or edited. Pages cite them.

-Date claims and cite the exact repository and commit for claims about code. Treat the wiki as a historical record. When a claim changes, add a dated successor and mark the old claim superseded without rewriting it.
+Three operations keep it alive:
+
+- **Ingest.** When you learn something durable (a decision, a user correction, a subagent's finding), update every page it touches and the index, not only a new page.
+- **Query.** Before a decision, and before briefing a subagent, read `index.md` and the pages it points to. If the answer you build is worth keeping, file it as a page.
+- **Lint.** Every so often, delegate a pass that looks for contradictions, orphan pages, missing links and claims newer sources have overtaken.
+
+### Write history, not the present
+
+The wiki is a historical record. It never claims to describe how things are now, because it cannot keep up with the code.
+
+- Date every claim: "On 2026-10-13, Matt decided..."
+- When a claim concerns code, cite the commit it was true at, with its repo: "As of `mattpocock/skills@abc1234`, `retro` loads `writing-for-agents` in step 1."
+- Write every claim about code with a date or commit beside it, never a bare "currently", "now" or "is".
+- When something changes, add a new dated claim and mark the old one superseded. Leave the old one as written.

 ## After friction

-After relaying a result that involved a retry, workaround, or blocked step, ask what would have made the work easier. If a narrower interface, a deterministic check, better evidence access, or a corrected convention addresses the cause, propose that change. Delegate it only after the user approves. Do not interrupt unrelated work to change the environment preemptively.
+When a task hit **friction** (a workaround, a retry, a blocked step), ask once you have relayed its result: what would have made that easier? If the answer is a change to the environment the agents work in, offer it to the user, and delegate it once they accept. Every change to your own setup and tools starts as an offer. The changes that pay off most:
+
+- **Constrained interfaces**: narrow APIs, lint rules that force correctness, coding standards a reviewer can enforce.
+- **Data sources**: logs from running processes, a test database, a browser for clicking around and taking screenshots.
+- **Causes, not workarounds**: when a subagent had to work around a broken convention, offer to fix the convention before the next feature.

### `-` → `docs/engineering/blast-radius.md`

@@ -1,37 +0,0 @@
-Quickstart:
-
-```bash
-npx skills add the-inconvenience-store/skills --skill=blast-radius
-```
-
-```bash
-npx skills update blast-radius
-```
-
-[Source](https://github.com/the-inconvenience-store/skills/tree/main/skills/blast-radius)
-
-## What it does
-
-`blast-radius` finds where a change could break a downstream consumer, shared state, or durable data. It tests the one **safety assumption** that makes the change safe on the exact source under review, or reports that assumption as unproven.
-
-## When to reach for it
-
-Type `/blast-radius`, or the agent reaches for it automatically when a task fits. Use it when a small-looking diff could have effects that a list of direct callers would miss. Use [code-review](https://aihero.dev/skills-code-review) for conformance to the spec and repo standards, or [verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-verify) to check whether the finished behavior works on its real surface.
-
-## Evidence beyond the diff
-
-A reader of old records might never call the writer you changed. The useful question is whether the reader can still handle records emitted by the new code. A focused run through that boundary can support or contradict the assumption. The report separates confirmed failure paths, cleared paths, and plausible paths that remain unchecked.
-
-## Common questions
-
-**Do I have to commit my changes first?**
-
-No. When using it on its own, tell it whether to include staged or working-tree changes. When called from [code-review](https://aihero.dev/skills-code-review), it keeps the review's pinned revision and diff scope. It does not switch refs or leave edits to the product.
-
-**What if the right version cannot be run safely?**
-
-The assumption is unproven. The report names the missing evidence rather than treating a check on a different revision or a mocked boundary as proof.
-
-## Where it fits
-
-`blast-radius` is a standalone risk check that [code-review](https://aihero.dev/skills-code-review) also uses for material risks. Its evidence stays separate from the review's Spec and Standards findings. Use [ask-inconvenient](https://aihero.dev/skills-ask-inconvenient) to choose a route.

### `-` → `docs/engineering/engineering-principles.md`

<details>

~~~~diff
--- local/docs/engineering/engineering-principles.md
+++ upstream/(absent)
@@ -1,89 +0,0 @@
-Quickstart:
-
-```bash
-npx skills add the-inconvenience-store/skills --skill=engineering-principles
-```
-
-```bash
-npx skills update engineering-principles
-```
-
-[Source](https://github.com/the-inconvenience-store/skills/tree/main/skills/engineering-principles)
-
-## What it does
-
-`engineering-principles` gives engineering workflows a shared vocabulary for recurring decisions: subtract before adding, model behavior structurally, keep retries idempotent, fail loudly, isolate parallel writers, and prove the real result without weakening the checks that prove it.
-
-The agent scans triggers against the decision in front of it, loads only references that could materially change it, and turns each into a concrete constraint, design choice, or proof obligation. References already available in context are reused across workflows; selection changes when a new material decision appears. You may name a principle for extra emphasis, but selection does not depend on you doing so.
-
-## When to reach for it
-
-Type `/engineering-principles`, or the agent reaches for it automatically while implementing, refactoring, reviewing, debugging, verifying, migrating, or dividing parallel work.
-
-Name a principle directly when you want to steer a decision: “use Subtract Before You Add,” “apply Boundary Discipline,” or “Prove It Works.” The name acts as a **leading word** that pulls in the full rule without making you repeat it. For module and seam vocabulary, use [codebase-design](https://aihero.dev/skills-codebase-design); for the project's domain language, use [domain-modeling](https://aihero.dev/skills-domain-modeling).
-
-## Defaults below evidence
-
-The principles sit below explicit product decisions, the accepted spec, repository standards, ADRs, and runtime evidence. They fill judgment gaps; they do not overturn recorded intent.
-
-This matters when useful principles pull in different directions. A one-wave API migration is simpler, but an independently deployed consumer may require bounded expand-contract. The skill preserves agreed behavior and a working feedback loop, then prefers the smaller reversible step. Deliberation scales with reversibility: a two-way door proceeds on precedent, while a one-way door such as data loss or a published contract earns exploration and confirmation.
-
-## Twenty-five leading words
-
-The index covers five families:
-
-- **Shape:** Laziness Protocol, Foundational Thinking, Redesign from First Principles, Subtract Before You Add, Minimize Reader Load, Outcome-Oriented Execution, Experience First, Exhaust the Design Space, and Build the Lever.
-- **Architecture:** Model Behavior Structurally, Boundary Discipline, Type System Discipline, Make Operations Idempotent, Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs, Separate Before Serializing Shared State, Treat Observable Behavior as Contract, and Fail Loudly.
-- **Verification:** Prove It Works, Protect the Signal, Fix Root Causes, Explain the Number, and Sequence Verifiable Units.
-- **Collaboration:** Guard the Context Window and Keep Execution Unblocked.
-- **Learning:** Encode Lessons in Structure.
-
-**Attack the Premise** is part of Fix Root Causes. When two fixes share an assumption and fail the same check, test that assumption directly before trying another. **Explain the Number** asks what result would change the decision and what the measurement actually counted, so a speedup claim reflects successful work rather than skipped work or noise.
-
-Two names are deliberately adapted to this workflow. **Model Behavior Structurally** leaves domain language to `domain-modeling`. **Keep Execution Unblocked** preserves the split that facts belong to the agent while product decisions belong to you.
-
-## Common questions
-
-**Do all twenty-five principles load every time?**
-
-No. The agent scans the index and reads only the leaves relevant to the decision. If you see a report citing most of the index, something has gone wrong with selection, not with the decision.
-
-**Will each workflow or subagent read the same references again?**
-
-A workflow reuses the selection and references already available in its context. After compaction, it reloads only selected references whose contents are missing. A fresh worker receives the relevant constraints, their rationale, and reference pointers, then selects for its own slice rather than inheriting the parent's whole reading list. It reads references for missing detail or additional decisions.
-
-**Does Prove It Works mean rerunning everything?**
-
-No. It asks for the least expensive evidence sufficient for the observable claim and repository requirements. The integration owner inspects delegated changes and validates their integration, reusing recorded checks only while their scope and inputs remain valid. Required fresh evidence still runs. If a broad run reveals a shared failure that makes further results uninformative, the agent stops it, diagnoses with focused checks, and resumes required broader coverage after the fix.
-
-**Do I have to name a principle for it to apply?**
-
-No. Selection is proactive: the workflows scan and load on their own, and naming one is an emphasis lever rather than a switch. Naming is worth doing when you want to force a particular reading of a decision: "use Subtract Before You Add" on a proposal that keeps growing, "Prove It Works" on a claim you don't believe yet. The name acts as a leading word that pulls in the whole rule without you restating it.
-
-**What happens when two principles disagree?**
-
-They are defaults, and they sit below evidence. Explicit product decisions, the accepted spec, repository standards, ADRs, and runtime evidence all outrank them, so a principle never overturns recorded intent. Where two principles genuinely pull against each other and nothing above them settles it, the skill preserves agreed behaviour and a working feedback loop first, then prefers the smaller reversible step. The worked example in the skill is migration shape: one wave is simpler, but an independently deployed consumer forces bounded expand-contract.
-
-**How is this different from `codebase-design`?**
-
-Both are vocabulary layers, and they answer different questions. [codebase-design](https://aihero.dev/skills-codebase-design) is about a module's *shape*: depth, interface, seam, adapter, leverage, locality. `engineering-principles` is about *decisions*: what to build, what to subtract, how to sequence a migration, what counts as proof. A design session usually wants both: the principles to decide, the design vocabulary to describe the result. [domain-modeling](https://aihero.dev/skills-domain-modeling) is the third layer, and it owns the project's own nouns.
-
-**Why do two of the names differ from the sources they come from?**
-
-To keep the boundaries between the vocabulary layers clean. **Model Behavior Structurally** stops short of naming things, because domain language belongs to `domain-modeling`. **Keep Execution Unblocked** preserves the split this whole set runs on: facts are the agent's job, product decisions are yours. A principle that quietly annexed a neighbouring skill's territory would make both harder to trust.
-
-**Nothing in the output mentioned a principle. Did it load at all?**
-
-Possibly, and that is the intended quiet case. Reports name a principle only when it resolved a conflict or drove a choice that would otherwise look arbitrary; a principle that merely agreed with the obvious decision earns no mention. If you want to see the selection, ask which triggers matched and why. A genuinely empty answer on a substantial change is worth pushing on.
-
-## It's working if
-
-- Relevant principles change visible engineering decisions without waiting for you to name them.
-- Only principles relevant to the current decision are loaded.
-- Existing specs, ADRs, and evidence remain authoritative.
-- Conditional rules state their boundary, such as atomic migration versus bounded expand-contract.
-- Reports name a principle only when it resolved a conflict or drove a non-obvious choice.
-
-## Where it fits
-
-`engineering-principles` is a **model-invoked vocabulary layer** beneath the engineering flow. [to-spec](https://aihero.dev/skills-to-spec), [to-tickets](https://aihero.dev/skills-to-tickets), [implement](https://aihero.dev/skills-implement), [diagnosing-bugs](https://aihero.dev/skills-diagnosing-bugs), [codebase-design](https://aihero.dev/skills-codebase-design), and [code-review](https://aihero.dev/skills-code-review) reach for the relevant principles at their own decision points. When you're unsure which skill or flow fits, [ask-inconvenient](https://aihero.dev/skills-ask-inconvenient) routes you.
~~~~

</details>

-Quickstart:
-

-

-npx skills update formal-verify
-```
-
-[Source](https://github.com/the-inconvenience-store/skills/tree/main/skills/formal-verify)
-
-## What it does
-
-`formal-verify` checks a named **property**, such as "retries with the same operation ID produce at most one durable write." It can check modeled event orders that tests rarely exercise, or use a verifier that analyzes the implementation itself.
-
-A verdict covers only the target and scope the tool actually checked. A model passing is a result about that model, not proof about the shipped code at the current revision.
-
-## When to reach for it
-
-Type `/formal-verify`, or the agent reaches for it automatically when you ask for formal proof or model checking, or when an existing project formal check applies to the change.
-
-Use it for a specific promise with costly failures that ordinary examples are unlikely to expose. To observe what happens through the shipped UI, CLI, service, or library, use [verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-verify) instead.
-
-## Prerequisites
-
-The selected checker must support the target and scope of the claim. Existing checks can be recorded under `docs/agents/formal-verification/`; without a record, Run uses a direct or scratch check if available. Only Create and Maintain write permanent verification files.
-
-## The property stays fixed
-
-Create records a reusable check and proves that a deliberate break makes the named property fail. Run checks the requested property at the revision under review. Maintain compares the check with current source, then repairs drift without rewriting a product bug as intended behavior. A check can be up to date and still correctly report a failure.
-
-## Common questions
-
-**Does a passing TLA+ model prove my implementation is right?**
-
-No. TLC explores the model under its configuration. A source correspondence review can show where the model applies, and a real-code replay can establish whether a reported schedule is possible in the implementation. If the claim is about what the actual code does for every input in a domain, use a code verifier that can analyze that code.
-
-**What if there is no verifier for my code, or the check only covers small inputs?**
-
-Generated-input tests on the implementation can still find bugs, but they are test evidence, not a formal verdict. A formal pass within a bound is useful evidence within that bound. A claim at every size needs evidence that covers every size.
-
-**Do I need a statechart?**
-
-No. A [statechart](https://aihero.dev/skills-statechart) is an optional view of the same checked model and configuration. Ask for one when a failing event sequence is easier to discuss as a path through states. The checker evidence, not the diagram, determines the verdict.
-
-## Where it fits
-
-`formal-verify` is a standalone tool for a specific formal obligation, not a default implementation gate. It complements [verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-verify), which proves behavior by driving the shipped surface. [ask-inconvenient](https://aihero.dev/skills-ask-inconvenient) routes you when the kind of evidence you need is unclear.
-
-The Create and Maintain branches adapt pstack's [Create Formal Verification](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/blob/b1fbf4b60ac6813b4583ccc356850dafcf492665/pstack/skills/create-formal-verification-skill/SKILL.md) and [Maintain Formal Verification](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/blob/b1fbf4b60ac6813b4583ccc356850dafcf492665/pstack/skills/maintain-formal-verification-skill/SKILL.md) from revision `b1fbf4b`.

### `-` → `docs/engineering/guardrails.md`

<details>
<summary><code>guardrails.md</code>: absent upstream</summary>


~~~~diff
--- local/docs/engineering/guardrails.md
+++ upstream/(absent)
@@ -1,97 +0,0 @@
-Quickstart:
-
-```bash
-npx skills add the-inconvenience-store/skills --skill=guardrails
-```
-
-```bash
-npx skills update guardrails
-```
-
-[Source](https://github.com/the-inconvenience-store/skills/tree/main/skills/guardrails)
-
-## What it does
-
-`guardrails` guides the setup of a project's linters, formatter, tests, reproducible installation, dependency upkeep, security scanning, CI checks, and hooks. It can start in an empty workspace or adapt an established repository without quietly replacing conventions that already work.
-
-The **proposal** is the control point: the agent investigates and recommends one coherent setup, then waits for you to approve or amend it before changing the project.
-
-For JavaScript, TypeScript, React, and Go, the skill carries curated rule baselines aimed at common agent-written failure modes. Those concrete recommendations feed the proposal; they are not installed wholesale without your approval. The skill is **generous** with lint coverage: it proposes every maintained linter, plugin, and rule group that applies to the stack, and leaves one out only for a named reason such as duplication, a formatter conflict, or hook runtime. When it sets up a JavaScript or TypeScript formatter (Prettier, oxfmt, or Biome), it starts from a house style: 2-space indent, 80-column width, trailing commas everywhere, no semicolons, single quotes in code, and double quotes in JSX.
-
-For TypeScript, it also recommends [Landmines](https://github.com/interfere-inc/landmines) (`@interfere/landmines`), an Oxlint plugin package targeting misleading tests, fixed sleeps, and flake masking. The proposal selects applicable rules rather than silently adopting the package's broader style and structure policies, and makes adding Oxlint explicit when the project does not already use it.
-
-For Ruby, C#, Rust, and other ecosystems without a bundled baseline, the agent researches current maintained tools and exact rules, then builds the equivalent proposal instead of skipping the language.
-
-For a new React application, it also offers a Bulletproof React-inspired standards package (feature boundaries, import direction, state and API conventions, and testing posture) as an explicit choice rather than an assumed architecture.
-
-## When to reach for it
-
-Type `/guardrails`, or the agent reaches for it automatically when a task fits.
-
-Reach for it when scaffolding a project, adding its first quality checks, replacing an unsatisfactory tool, or bringing inconsistent lint and hook configuration back under control. For configuring the issue tracker and documentation expected by this collection's engineering flows, use [bootstrap-skills](https://aihero.dev/skills-bootstrap-skills) instead.
-
-## Guardrails with boundaries
-
-The skill separates fast local feedback from the complete CI gate. It keeps local hooks focused, makes slower checks explicit, and treats architecture rules, coverage, commit policy, and agent-specific hooks as choices rather than surprise additions. When git hooks are in scope, it asks whether you want Conventional Commits enforced on `commit-msg`: commitlint for JavaScript and TypeScript repos, cocogitto for everything else.
-
-It can also set up or reuse an optional task runner, then make its `bootstrap`, `check`, and `codegen` tasks the shared interface where those jobs apply. Without a task runner, it keeps the project's native commands instead of adding task aliases.
-
-When the project needs them, the proposal also covers a real test baseline, generated-code drift checks, locked installation, dependency audits and update automation, and proof that a fresh checkout can pass the complete gate. Update bots and other workflow changes remain explicit choices.
-
-## Security scanning at commit time
-
-Semgrep and Gitleaks are optional, but recommended when agents commit to the repo. They run as **pre-commit** hooks on staged changes, so an injectable query, disabled TLS check, or pasted API key is caught at the commit that introduces it rather than at review. CI runs the same scans as the backstop. Semgrep's rules are committed to the repo so the hook works offline and stays fast. They include a small set of project rules aimed at mistakes agents commonly make, each with a message naming the safe alternative. Registry rules are vendored only into private repos, because their license forbids redistribution; public repos fetch those packs in CI instead.
-
-Verification is proportionate: commands are run, representative failures are demonstrated safely, and anything that would require commits, merges, installs, or other side effects is left unverified unless you approve it.
-
-## Common questions
-
-**Will it rip out the tooling I already have?**
-
-Not without saying so. Existing tools are either preserved or replaced for a stated reason, and the reason lands in the proposal before anything changes. The proposal is the whole control point: the agent investigates, recommends one coherent setup, and waits. If you want a specific tool kept, say so at that step rather than after.
-
-**My language isn't JavaScript, TypeScript, React or Go. Does it skip me?**
-
-No. Those four ship with curated rule baselines aimed at the failure modes agents actually produce, so the proposal for them is concrete out of the box. For Ruby, C#, Rust and anything else, the agent researches the currently maintained tools and the exact rules, then builds the equivalent proposal. The output shape is the same; what differs is whether the recommendation came from a bundled baseline or from research the agent did in front of you. Research is worth reading more carefully than a baseline.
-
-**Why are the pre-commit hooks so thin? I wanted the full suite to run.**
-
-Because a slow hook gets bypassed, and a bypassed hook guards nothing. The skill deliberately splits fast local feedback from the complete gate: hooks stay quick, CI owns the full run, and the boundary between them is made visible rather than left implicit. If you genuinely want the whole suite locally, ask for it in the proposal. It is a choice, not a prohibition.
-
-**It said it couldn't verify part of what it set up.**
-
-That is the skill being honest rather than failing. Verification is proportionate: commands get run and representative failures get demonstrated safely, but anything needing a commit, a merge, an install, or another real side effect is left unverified unless you approve it. A report that names an unverified path is more useful than one that claims a green CI run it never triggered. The same applies to failures that were already there before it started: those get reported, not quietly absorbed.
-
-**Why do the security scans run on pre-commit when other slow checks get pushed to CI?**
-
-Because the point is to catch the problem before it lands in history, where a leaked secret is already leaked. Both tools scan only staged files: Gitleaks is a single fast binary, and Semgrep uses committed rules with no network calls. The hook's runtime is measured during setup. If Semgrep goes over budget, the slowest rule packs move to CI and the rest stay in the hook.
-
-**Does it catch dead code?**
-
-Yes, as an optional whole-project CI scan on top of the per-file unused-variable rules. TypeScript repos get [Knip](https://knip.dev) for unused files, exports, and dependencies. Go modules that build a binary get `deadcode`, which reports functions unreachable from `main`, including exported ones that `unused` cannot see. Both tools judge reachability from configured entry points, so the agent sets those up explicitly, and an established repo gets a baseline rather than a wall of failures.
-
-**How is this different from `bootstrap-skills`?**
-
-Different subject. [bootstrap-skills](https://aihero.dev/skills-bootstrap-skills) configures what the *skills* need (the issue tracker, the triage labels, the domain-doc layout) and then invokes this one. `guardrails` configures what the *project* needs: lint, format, tests, reproducible install, dependency upkeep, CI, hooks. Running the setup skill gets you both. Run `guardrails` on its own when only the quality strategy is changing.
-
-**When do I run it again?**
-
-When the stack changes or the quality strategy does: a new language in the repo, a formatter swap, a move from ad-hoc scripts to a task runner, a CI provider change. [retro](https://aihero.dev/skills-retro) is the other common route in: when a session's finding turns out to be "this repo has no baseline at all", that is a `guardrails` run rather than one more lint rule.
-
-**Does the Bulletproof React package come as standard on a React app?**
-
-No. It is offered as an explicit choice, and only for a new React application. Feature boundaries, import direction, state and API conventions and testing posture are opinionated enough that inheriting them by accident would be worse than not having them. Decline it and the rest of the proposal stands unchanged.
-
-## It's working if
-
-- The approved lint and format commands cover every detected ecosystem, or the report names a researched coverage gap.
-- Existing tools were preserved or replaced for a stated reason.
-- Local hooks are fast, CI owns the complete gate, and each boundary is visible.
-- A fresh checkout has a defined locked setup-and-check path, even when that path could not be exercised safely during setup.
-- Generated code and dependency updates have clear commands and ownership when the project uses them.
-- When security scanning was accepted, a staged vulnerable pattern or fake secret is blocked at commit with a message saying what to do instead.
-- Pre-existing failures and unverified behavior are reported rather than hidden.
-
-## Where it fits
-
-`guardrails` is a run-once setup, repeated when the stack or quality strategy changes. [bootstrap-skills](https://aihero.dev/skills-bootstrap-skills) invokes it after recording repository configuration, then invokes [verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-verify) against the resulting launch and check commands. Downstream skills such as [implement](https://aihero.dev/skills-implement) work inside the approved guardrails. [Ask Inconvenient](https://aihero.dev/skills-ask-inconvenient) maps the full collection.
~~~~

</details>

-```text
-/parity Implement the page editor from ~/Desktop/cOS/pages.
-Use the exported HTML and supplied screenshots as the references,
-including the phone layout and save/conflict states.
-Reuse this project's design-system components.
-```
-
-## Prerequisites
-
-Provide an existing project and accessible design references. The agent needs browser or equivalent surface-driving tools to inspect runnable references and the actual application. Runtime or access gaps are reported as unverified, not replaced with a claim based on code inspection.
-
-## A fixed baseline
-
-The baseline makes **parity** checkable. Reading exported code explains its structure and values; rendering it reveals the actual result. When both are available, the skill requires both, as well as opening supplied images.
-
-Comparisons pair the same screen, state, viewport, and content. A first pass across the requested screens identifies corrections before broad validation. The agent batches fixes and refreshes only affected captures, preserving successful evidence until a relevant change invalidates it. In-scope differences still require correction or your explicit acceptance.
-
-## A visual loop, not a release framework
-
-Project instructions own testing, review, commits, and deployment. `parity` adds no mandatory principle scan, TDD orchestration, or separate verification-skill phase. Unless project policy says otherwise, affected checks run during corrections and broad checks run once the UI is visually coherent.
-
-Missing backend capabilities, unrelated bugs, and infrastructure failures are reported separately. They do not automatically expand the task. A failure that prevents observing a requested screen leaves that screen blocked, not falsely verified.
-
-## Common questions
-
-**Is this tied to Claude Design exports?**
-
-No. Claude Design folders and ZIPs are one input path. Screenshots, other runnable exports, design-tool files, and live pages can also supply the reference. A screenshot proves only the visible state; hidden behavior and unsupplied responsive layouts are not treated as observed facts.
-
-**What if the design conflicts with the project's components?**
-
-The agent first reuses or appropriately extends existing components. If a design-system constraint prevents a match, it names the conflict and asks for a decision rather than quietly sacrificing fidelity or creating a parallel component system.
-
-**How is this different from `/implement` or the upstream `/match`?**
-
-`implement` starts from settled behavior and test seams. `parity` supplies the visual inspection, implementation, and correction loop. Use it directly for design reproduction; when you explicitly combine it with `implement`, the enclosing workflow runs engineering gates once. It is inspired by [match](https://github.com/raphaelsalaja/skills/tree/main/skills/match), with handling for export folders, source-plus-render inspection, and project component reuse.
-
-**Does it promise pixel-perfect results everywhere?**
-
-Only inspected viewports and states can support a parity claim. Screenshot-derived measurements remain estimates, and inferred responsive behavior is identified separately. The report includes paired captures, accepted deviations, and any missing observations.
-
-**Will it implement backend functionality implied by the mockup?**
-
-Only when explicitly in scope. It identifies missing capabilities early and continues independent visual work while a decision is pending. Approving one feature does not approve every other feature later discovered in the references.
-
-**Does every fix restart verification?**
-
-No. Only affected captures, interactions, and checks become stale. Final proof closes remaining gaps instead of repeating successful work. Unrelated findings are reported separately rather than absorbed into an unbounded repair cycle.
-
-## It's working if
-
-- The agent inspects the references and captures the baseline before production edits.
-- Implementation captures are paired with the reference at matching sizes and states.
-- Visible discrepancies cause fixes and fresh comparisons.
-- The final report includes comparison evidence and real-surface behavior verification.
-
-## Where it fits
-
-`parity` is a standalone visual implementation loop that can also supplement an explicitly invoked [implement](https://aihero.dev/skills-implement) workflow without duplicating its engineering gates. For the wider map, use [ask-inconvenient](https://aihero.dev/skills-ask-inconvenient).
~~~~

</details>

-
-```bash
-npx skills update ship
-```
-
-[Source](https://github.com/the-inconvenience-store/skills/tree/main/skills/ship)
-
-## What it does
-
-`ship` takes finished branch work to an open pull request: it rebases onto the fetched `main` or `master`, resolves conflicts, verifies the result, commits remaining work, and pushes. It uses [pr](https://aihero.dev/skills-pr) to shape the body before publishing it.
-
-Shipping stops at a **review-ready** PR, not a merge. The workflow preserves unrelated work and reconciles upstream intent rather than treating conflict resolution as choosing a side.
-
-## When to reach for it
-
-You invoke this by typing `/ship`, and the agent won't reach for it on its own. Use it when your implementation is ready to publish but still needs integration with the base branch. For the PR body alone, use [pr](https://aihero.dev/skills-pr).
-
-## Prerequisites
-
-A Git repository with a reachable `main` or `master`, push access to the working branch's remote, and an authenticated CLI or API for the hosting platform. Install `pr` alongside `ship`.
-
-## Review-ready
-
-Rebasing can change behavior even when Git reports no conflicts. Verification covers the integrated result before publication. A published branch that needs history rewritten gets an explicit force-with-lease tied to the remote commit observed before rebasing, so another contributor's intervening push is not silently overwritten.
-
-Uncommitted work owned by the task is saved and restored across the rebase. Unrelated changes stay untouched; if they prevent a clean rebase, the agent pauses for isolation instead of sweeping them into a stash or commit.
-
-## Common questions
-
-**Does it replace `pr`?**
-
-No. `ship` handles branch integration and publication; `pr` owns the body format and evidence presentation.
-
-**Does it merge the PR?**
-
-No. The endpoint is an open PR with a confirmed URL. An existing open PR for the same head and base is updated rather than duplicated.
-
-**What happens when a conflict needs a decision?**
-
-The agent resolves conflicts whose intended behavior is supported by the code and conversation. It asks when a product decision is missing and keeps the work recoverable. Failed required checks block publication unless you explicitly accept them.
-
-## Where it fits
-
-`ship` is the publication **chain step** after [implement](https://aihero.dev/skills-implement). It delegates the review presentation to [pr](https://aihero.dev/skills-pr). See [ask-inconvenient](https://aihero.dev/skills-ask-inconvenient) for the full flow.
~~~~

</details>

-Quickstart:

-
-```bash
-npx skills update statechart
-```
-
-[Source](https://github.com/the-inconvenience-store/skills/tree/main/skills/statechart)
-
-## What it does
-
-Statechart turns a TLA+ model of a product flow, protocol, or service into a Mermaid statechart. The arrows come from states and transitions TLC actually explored in the model, not from a diagram sketched by the agent. The agent puts the states and actions into words the reader can judge.
-
-## When to reach for it
-
-Type `/statechart`, or the agent reaches for it automatically when a task calls for a model-based statechart or a visual explanation of a counterexample. Reach for it when someone needs to see what can happen next or how a modeled rule breaks. Use [formal-verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-formal-verify) when the main question is which rules hold for a bounded model, and [verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-verify) when the main question is what the running implementation does.
-
-## Prerequisites
-
-The chart runner needs Node 22.18 to 22.x, Node 23.6 or later, Bun 1.1.5 or later, or Deno 2.0 or later. It needs mise and network access on the first run unless you point it at an existing TLC jar and Java 11 or later. SVG output also needs Node and npm; the renderer is installed in scratch only when needed.
-
-## Show the path, not just the bad state
-
-A counterexample is a sequence of actions, not just a red box. The report names the rule and gives TLC's path to the violation, so the reader can see what actually leads there. If the chart groups model states together, it distinguishes states that break a rule from states that only sometimes break it.
-
-## Common questions
-
-**Do I need a formal-verify run first?** No. Statechart can use an existing TLA+ model and config or help you write them. If formal-verify hands off a model, the chart uses exactly the spec and config it checked.
-
-**Why did I get a report but no full chart?** Above 500 states, the runner draws only counterexample paths. If there are no violations to draw, it produces the report without a Mermaid file.
-
-**Does a counterexample prove the shipped code has a bug?** No. It shows how a rule breaks in that model and configuration. Replay the path against the implementation before calling it a real bug.
-
-## Where it fits
-
-Statechart is a standalone tool for reviewing stateful behavior. It can also present [formal-verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-formal-verify) findings from the same model, while [verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-verify) can supply real-surface evidence when a path needs replay. Browse the full map in [ask-inconvenient](https://aihero.dev/skills-ask-inconvenient).
~~~~

</details>

### `-` → `docs/engineering/verify.md`

<details>
<summary><code>verify.md</code>: absent upstream</summary>


~~~~diff
--- local/docs/engineering/verify.md
+++ upstream/(absent)
@@ -1,91 +0,0 @@
-Quickstart:
-
-```bash
-npx skills add the-inconvenience-store/skills --skill=verify
-```
-
-```bash
-npx skills update verify
-```
-
-[Source](https://github.com/the-inconvenience-store/skills/tree/main/skills/verify)
-
-## What it does
-
-`verify` proves behavior through the **real surface** a user or consumer touches: the running UI, CLI, service, mobile app, or public library interface.
-
-It does not treat compilation, tests, screenshots without actions, or an agent's report as proof of the changed behavior. It drives the public path, observes its result and durable side effects, and returns `VERIFIED`, `NOT VERIFIED`, or `INCONCLUSIVE`.
-
-## When to reach for it
-
-Type `/verify`, or the agent reaches for it automatically when a task needs real-surface evidence.
-
-Reach for it to prove a completed change, to create a repeatable project-local driving route, or to audit existing verification instructions after the application changes. During implementation the agent uses its Run branch; creation and maintenance happen only when that is the requested job.
-
-## Prerequisites
-
-Run mode uses project instructions under `docs/agents/verification/` when they exist. Without them, the skill performs the strongest direct check the repository and available tools support, reports the missing reusable route, and leaves permanent project files untouched.
-
-## Three branches, one contract
-
-**Create** learns how the repository actually launches and exposes its user-facing surfaces, writes portable instructions and feature maps, then proves one mapped feature by following those instructions cold.
-
-**Run** selects the changed behavior, health-checks a known instance, drives the public path, captures the action and result, checks promised side effects, and cleans up what it started without deleting evidence. A path longer than a handful of interactions is written as one scratch script and run in a single call, then named as a candidate route for Maintain to promote.
-
-**Maintain** compares every mapped feature with source and then drives every feature live. Documentation and owned harness drift are corrected; a product regression is reported rather than rewritten as intended behavior.
-
-All three branches share one project format, so creation and maintenance cannot quietly teach different verification standards.
-
-Browser verification runs headlessly unless you explicitly request a headed browser. Each browser surface's project instructions record the headless launch configuration; a path that cannot run headlessly stays unverified rather than triggering an automatic switch to a visible browser.
-
-## Proof, not a proxy
-
-The leading word is **proof**. A valid proof exercises the shipped path and observes what the consumer was promised. A test can preserve that contract and a typecheck can rule out a class of mistakes, but neither establishes that the running surface launches, accepts the interaction, and produces the promised state.
-
-An inconclusive observation stays inconclusive. The skill never rounds it up because nearby checks passed.
-
-## Common questions
-
-**Was this called `verification`?**
-
-Yes. The skill is now `verify`; invoke `/verify` and install or update it under the new name. The project artifact remains at `docs/agents/verification/`.
-
-**Isn't this what my end-to-end tests already do?**
-
-Not quite, and the difference is what is being proved. An end-to-end test proves that a scripted path held the last time CI ran it, against whatever fixtures and stubs the suite installs. `verify` proves that *this* change, on the surface as shipped, launches, accepts the interaction, and produces the promised state, now. The two are complementary, and the skill says so: a test preserves behaviour at a seam, verification proves the application path. If your e2e suite genuinely drives the real surface, say so in `docs/agents/verification/` and let Run invoke it; the skill is not precious about the mechanism, only about what gets observed.
-
-**It came back `INCONCLUSIVE` and everything else passed. Can I treat that as done?**
-
-No, and that is the one rule the skill will not bend. An inconclusive observation stays inconclusive; it is never rounded up because the typecheck passed or the tests are green. The useful thing is what `INCONCLUSIVE` carries with it: the exact gap that stopped the observation. That is usually a missing launch step, a surface with no mapped route, or a side effect nobody wrote down. Fix the gap and rerun rather than arguing with the verdict. Both [implement](https://aihero.dev/skills-implement) and [diagnosing-bugs](https://aihero.dev/skills-diagnosing-bugs) treat `INCONCLUSIVE` as incomplete for the same reason.
-
-**I don't have `docs/agents/verification/`. Does Run just fail?**
-
-No. It performs the strongest direct check the repository and the available tools support, reports that there is no reusable route, and leaves permanent project files alone. That last part is deliberate: a Run invocation is not allowed to quietly become a Create invocation and write a half-learned route into your repo. When you do want the route, ask for it and the skill takes the Create branch, which learns how the repo launches, writes the instructions, and then proves one mapped feature by following them cold.
-
-**`verify` took hundreds of browser steps and hours of agent time.**
-
-Each interaction driven as its own agent action costs a full model turn, so a long flow driven click by click is slow even when every click is fast. Run now writes a path longer than a handful of interactions as one scratch script and runs it in a single call, rerunning the same script after a fix. The script stays scratch during Run; the verdict names it so a Maintain pass can promote it into `docs/agents/verification/`.
-
-**Why does Create insist on proving a feature before it finishes?**
-
-Because instructions nobody has followed are a guess. The cold run is the completion criterion: it catches the launch step that only works because your shell already had the environment variable, the port that was already bound, the command that needs a build first. A route that has never been walked is the commonest way verification documentation goes stale before it is even committed.
-
-**My app has no UI. Does this apply?**
-
-Yes. The real surface is whatever the consumer touches: a CLI's argv and stdout, a service's HTTP endpoint, a library's public exports, a mobile app's screens. The skill is written around the public path and the observable result, not around a browser. A library's verification is a consumer calling the published interface and getting the promised value back.
-
-**Maintain found something broken. Will it just update the feature map?**
-
-Only for drift it owns: documentation that no longer matches the source, or a harness the skill itself wrote. A product regression gets reported, not rewritten as intended behaviour. This is the failure mode the split exists to prevent: a maintenance pass that quietly redefines a bug as the spec, leaving the feature map green and the product broken.
-
-## It's working if
-
-- The final report names the public path and the observed result.
-- Evidence shows the action as well as the resulting state.
-- Promised files, records, messages, or other side effects are checked.
-- Failed attempts leave no stale process or scratch state behind.
-- Product regressions are reported instead of absorbed into the feature map.
-
-## Where it fits
-
-`verify` is bootstrapped by [bootstrap-skills](https://aihero.dev/skills-bootstrap-skills) after [guardrails](https://aihero.dev/skills-guardrails) establishes the repository's final launch and check commands. It then serves as the real-surface completion gate after [implement](https://aihero.dev/skills-implement) and the reusable driving route that [diagnosing-bugs](https://aihero.dev/skills-diagnosing-bugs) can use to construct and rerun a bug-specific feedback loop. It complements [tdd](https://aihero.dev/skills-tdd): tests preserve behavior at a seam; verification proves the actual application path. When you're unsure which skill or flow fits, [ask-inconvenient](https://aihero.dev/skills-ask-inconvenient) routes you.
~~~~

</details>

-## What it does
-
-`why` investigates the rationale for an existing design, historical change, or measured threshold. It treats what the code does as a lead, not as evidence of what its authors intended.
-
-## When to reach for it
-
-Type `/why`, or the agent reaches for it automatically when a task fits. Use it to ask what tradeoff led to a decision, what evidence set a threshold, or what changed in the history of a reproduced regression. Use [how](https://aihero.dev/skills-how) if you want to trace current behavior instead.
-
-## What the record can tell you
-
-A **recorded** reason comes from a cited primary record, such as the PR discussion that explains a decision or measurements that justify a threshold. An **inferred** reason fits the evidence but was not stated. An **unknown** is a question the available record leaves open.
-
-For a recent agent-authored change, `why` also looks for the conversation that led to it. It matches the conversation to the actual edit and distinguishes the user's decision from the agent's proposal.
-
-## Common questions
-
-**What if there is no decision record?**
-
-A commit message, issue, PR discussion, measurement, or relevant agent conversation can still carry the reason. If the history is inaccessible or cannot be linked to the change, the answer makes that gap explicit rather than presenting an inference as intent.
-
-**Can history establish the cause of a bug?**
-
-Finding a candidate change can inform a hypothesis. It does not reproduce the reported behavior or test that hypothesis. Start with [diagnosing-bugs](https://aihero.dev/skills-diagnosing-bugs) when something is failing now.
-
-## Where it fits
-
-`why` is a standalone, read-only historical investigation. [diagnosing-bugs](https://aihero.dev/skills-diagnosing-bugs) can use its findings after reproduction when history might change the next hypothesis. Use [ask-inconvenient](https://aihero.dev/skills-ask-inconvenient) to choose a route.

-## What it does

-

-
-## Load-bearing words
-
-A term is **load-bearing** if using it changes the request. For example, “support retries” could mean recovering interrupted work, or it could mean preventing a second charge when someone resends a payment request. The useful distinction is what the system must do in each case, not which wording sounds more technical.

-
-**What if it can't verify a precedent or tell which problem I mean?**

-## Where it fits

 ## What it does

-`ask-inconvenient` starts with what you want to do, not the name of a skill. It recommends the next command, explains why, and can give you a prompt ready to send. It mentions setup only when it changes that next step.
+`ask-matt` is the router over the skills in this repo. You describe the situation you are in (an idea you cannot start, a pile of incoming bug reports, a [session](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/session) that has run long), and it names the skill or the sequence of skills that fits, plus where the human decisions in that sequence sit.

-It **does no work itself**. It doesn't grill, write a spec, or fix anything; it only orients. It exists for the user-invoked skills above all: nothing fires those for you, so `ask-inconvenient` is the memory you offload that to. It also maps model-invoked disciplines such as [verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-verify) and the three vocabulary layers: [domain-modeling](https://aihero.dev/skills-domain-modeling), [codebase-design](https://aihero.dev/skills-codebase-design), and [engineering-principles](https://aihero.dev/skills-engineering-principles).
+It recommends and stops. It does not grill, write a [spec](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/spec), open a file or fire the skill it just named; what you get back is the next thing to type, and you type it. It is also a hand-written map of the skills in this repo rather than a scan of what you have installed, so it will not route you over your own skills or another author's.

 ## When to reach for it

-You invoke this by typing `/ask-inconvenient`; the agent won't reach for it on its own.
+You invoke this by typing `/ask-matt`; the agent won't reach for it on its own.

 | Your situation | What the router gives back |
 | --- | --- |
-| An engineering task to run without picking the workflow | [inconvenient-mode](https://aihero.dev/skills-inconvenient-mode), which does the authorized work instead of recommending a command |
-| What the code does now, or why someone designed it that way | [how](https://aihero.dev/skills-how) traces the current code; [why](https://aihero.dev/skills-why) traces the decision record |
-| An unclear idea needs the right vocabulary before design starts | [reframe](https://aihero.dev/skills-reframe), for checked precedents and a rewritten brief |
-| A scoped task prompt needs better sources, methods, or proof | [sharpen](https://aihero.dev/skills-sharpen), without expanding or doing the task |
-| A change looks small but could break a consumer elsewhere | [blast-radius](https://aihero.dev/skills-blast-radius), for a focused check of the safety assumption |
-| Progress in this chat, and what decisions still need you | [ketchup](https://aihero.dev/skills-ketchup), not [handoff](https://aihero.dev/skills-handoff) for another agent or [wait-what](https://aihero.dev/skills-wait-what) for one confusing reply |
-| Work on a topic is scattered across earlier chats | [recall](https://aihero.dev/skills-recall), which checks what still holds against current project records |
-| A long run needs a record of what was decided and why | [show-me-your-work](https://aihero.dev/skills-show-me-your-work), for an append-only trail linked to evidence |
-| An idea, and no idea where to start | The head of the main flow, including whether a spec earns its cost |
-| Incoming bugs and requests | The [triage](https://aihero.dev/skills-triage) on-ramp, not another triage pass over tickets you generated yourself |
-| Supplied designs to reproduce in the existing app | [parity](https://aihero.dev/skills-parity), with reference captures and a visual correction loop |
-| A named property should hold across event orders or inputs | [formal-verify](https://aihero.dev/skills-formal-verify) to create, run, or maintain a check with explicit scope |
-| A transition model or counterexample needs a readable chart | [statechart](https://aihero.dev/skills-statechart) to generate it from TLC output |
-| Finished branch work to publish | [ship](https://aihero.dev/skills-ship) to rebase, resolve conflicts, verify, commit, push, and open a PR using [pr](https://aihero.dev/skills-pr) |
-| Two skills that look interchangeable | A concrete boundary: working directory or none, single-session or multi-session planning |
-| A long session and a context decision | The ordered choices at a phase boundary |
-| A session, repeated agent mistake, or ineffective skill to learn from | [retro](https://aihero.dev/skills-retro) for proposals; `/retro time` if you want measured time accounting |
-| Engineering docs need a structure, or a draft just needs cleaner prose | [technical-writing](https://aihero.dev/skills-technical-writing) for structure; [unslop](https://aihero.dev/skills-unslop) for a copy pass |
-| A skill you have already picked | No extra step needed. Invoke that skill directly. |

 ## Prerequisites

-The router does not install the skills it recommends. Install the ones you intend to use; this is a hand-maintained map of this repo, not a scan of every skill on your machine. Tracker-dependent routes also need [bootstrap-skills](https://aihero.dev/skills-bootstrap-skills) to configure the repo first.
+The router names skills; it does not install them. Everything it points at has to be installed for the recommendation to be actionable, and it only knows the promoted skills in this repo.
